aqueous systems, we have observed that low surface tension solvents (e.g., acetonitrile) readily leak at the gasket interfaces, often
evinced by dried active species or solvent accumulating on the gasket periphery within a few hours). Expanded PTFE (ePTFE—e.g.,
Gore tape), by contrast, provides improved sealing for such solvents due to its compressibility; however, expanded PTFE gaskets cannot
be reliably reused after compression.
   Creep deformation, like with the polypropylene diffuser, might be concerning for longer-duration operation of a flow cell [59].
While the above-proposed backing plate helps maintain effective sealing by limiting the degree of polypropylene diffuser creep, the
PTFE gaskets themselves may deform with time and cause leaks days or weeks into operation. Longer operation may be achieved with
more compressible and lower durometer materials such as ePTFE or EPDM.

2.5. Electrodes and separators/membranes

   The design choice of stackable gaskets accommodates a wide range of electrode thicknesses, enabling testing of both novel con­
structs and commercial standards. For this flow cell, porous graphitic electrodes, such as carbon papers, felts, and cloths, which can be

                                                                4T.R. Goodwin et al.                                                                                                 HardwareX 28 (2026) e00834

functionalized with catalysts through a variety of methods, are mostly commonly implemented. Metal foams and meshes are also
compatible with this architecture. In addition, the flow cell readily supports small-area, nonstandard electrodes, such as those
fabricated via non-solvent induced phase separation (NIPS) and electrospinning [22,34].
  A wide variety of membranes or separators can be utilized. The membrane or separator is positioned between two gaskets; because
there is no dedicated cavity for this component, sealing is achieved by either (1) compression on the membrane itself such that
electrolyte does not pass through its pores at the gasket-membrane interface or (2) deformation of the gasket stack around the region
not covered by the membrane. Consequently, the maximum usable thickness of the membrane or separator depends on  its
compressibility and that of the gasket to conform around it. In practice, this flow cell accommodates separators and membranes
ranging in thickness from ca. 10 μm to 1 mm, including commercial offerings such as Celgard, Daramic, Nafion, and Fumasep. This
platform is also compatible with bespoke or emerging separators, membranes, and composites (e.g., ceramic composite membranes)
[39,60].

2.6.  Critical balance of plant

   At minimum, the flow cell must be connected to tubing, a pump, an electrolyte reservoir, and a potentiostat. While there are many
pumps available to which satisfy different operating requirements (e.g., pulsing behavior, flow rates, efficiency, pressure envelopes),
peristaltic pumps are frequently employed due to their ease of use and simplicity in exchanging the tubing components that are wetted.
Diaphragm pumps are another common choice, which may be preferred for certain applications because of the different mechanism of
operation (e.g., avoiding oscillations at low flow rates, reducing mechanical wear on tubing).
   Tubing should be chemically compatible with the electrolyte(s). For small electrolyte volumes (on the order of 10 mL and smaller),
long lengths should be avoided and, if possible, the diameter restricted (e.g., < 1/16″ ID) to minimize holdup. While it is possible to
employ a wide range of tubing for peristaltic pumps, those not designed for such purposes may disintegrate faster and lead to leaks.
Still, even well-designed tubing can leak. To facilitate easy replacement at the most-likely failure point (i.e., the section of tubing
compressed in the peristaltic pump), tubing is frequently divided into multiple sections, with one section dedicated for the peristaltic
pump head (e.g., norprene tubing), and the other sections of (often less-expensive) tubing selected for completing the fluidic circuit (e.
g., teflon or polypropylene tubing).
   Electrolyte reservoirs vary in size and function. Critical considerations might include volume, material(s) of construction (for
chemical compatibility, thermal tolerance), pressure rating, aspect ratio (as large diameter:height ratios may be challenging), and
options for ports (i.e., inlet/outlet, instrumentation connections). Often, we employ glass reservoirs with open lids for acidic or neutral
systems and polypropylene reservoirs for alkaline systems. Using hole punches, gaskets can be cut from materials compatible with
electrolyte (e.g., EPDM) to accommodate tubing for the inlet and outlet flow paths as well as for inert gases (vide infra); it is often best to
place the inlets on the opposite side of the reservoir from the outlets to avoid bypassing the bulk volume (e.g., inlet at bottom, outlet at
top). Additionally, stir bars can be implemented to ensure homogeneous concentrations within the reservoir. Improved sealing ap­
paratuses are sometimes needed for chemistries employing solvents that readily evaporate. For non-aqueous systems that require
sealing, we often employ 10 mL volume molded perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) jars (Savillex, 102–0010-01). More specialized reservoirs can
be used to address advanced challenges with flow cell use (e.g., removing headspace for gas to prevent volume imbalance).
    Finally, equipment to control the current or voltage supplied to the cell is required. Our device of choice is a potentiostat, which can
reliably perform many electrochemical methods useful in the analysis of cell performance. Increased precision, higher current
capability, access to a broader range of techniques, more mature software interfaces, and integration with dedicated instrument
ecosystems tend to correlate with higher costs. Alternatively, more affordable equipment, like a battery cycler or a power source, can
be used depending on the application of the flow cell.

2.7.  Alternative and additional ancillaries

   The preceding sections describe the basic needs  for operation. In certain  cases, additional equipment  is required  for
experiments—we briefly discuss some of these here to ensure adequate consideration of necessary componentry for a distribution of
experiments and to support more advanced campaigns. Gases are often supplied to the head space of the reservoirs or sparged into the
electrolyte. Humidifiers, vessels containing the same solvent to that of the electrolyte and a gas sparger, can be used to pre-saturate the
gas with solvent vapor to minimize evaporation from the electrolyte tank(s). Sensors installed in reservoirs or inline to tubing can offer
information about the electrolyte during operation [61]. Such measurements might include conductivity, spectroscopy, or mass-
transport limited concentration measurement (e.g., via ultramicroelectrode), amongst others. The specific need and applicability of
each of these techniques depends on the target research question, the chemistry, and sometimes the scale of the system (e.g., smaller-
volume systems can be more difficult to instrument). Exchange of certain components and/or modifications to materials or func­
tionality can also expand the type of and/or elevate the quality of data obtained from the cell. For instance, variants of the diffuser
design have been developed to implement reference electrodes and to facilitate elevated temperature operation by using a combination
of thermocouples, heating elements such as patch or cartridge heaters, and a feedback temperature controller [20,62]. Further, the
inlet and outlet ports might be replaced with alternative fittings to ensure gas-tight seals and facilitate elevated-pressure operation
[63]. The flow cell might be placed in dedicated enclosures to keep it in an inert environment (e.g., glovebox). Filters can be used to
prevent accumulation of solids in the system, which might damage the flow cell, pumps, and/or impede flow. Other choices are
described in earlier sections, and additional possibilities extend beyond those discussed here.

## pqac-00000029

From text 'wen2021lasersurfacetreatment pages 17-22'.

Haifang Wen. Laser surface treatment and laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing study using custom designed 3d printer and the application of machine learning in materials science. Unknown journal, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.31390/gradschool\_dissertations.5640, doi:10.31390/gradschool\_dissertations.5640.

The excerpt identifies the LSU custom LPBF system’s powder chamber as an 8 × 4 × 2 inch solid aluminum block. It was CNC-machined at the LSU machine shop, indicating that fabrication of this chamber was performed in-house rather than outsourced. Other structural parts, including the aluminum plates and rail components, were also cut or machined at the LSU machine shop, although some commercial components were purchased from suppliers such as McMaster-Carr. Practical fabrication and assembly challenges included achieving correct alignment and smooth motion of the powder-handling mechanism. The platforms required felt seals against the chamber walls to prevent metal powder from becoming trapped between the platform and wall and causing the platforms to stick. The wiper blade rails had to be installed at the same height and adjusted so that the blade sat approximately 25 micrometers above the powder-chamber surface. Assembly had to proceed from the bottom upward, with careful checks of the rail levels, spacing, and step-motor movement to ensure proper wiper operation. The excerpt does not report major machining failures or outsourced fabrication; instead, it emphasizes dimensional adjustment, sealing against powder contamination, and alignment during assembly.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'wen2021lasersurfacetreatment pages 22-27'.

Haifang Wen. Laser surface treatment and laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing study using custom designed 3d printer and the application of machine learning in materials science. Unknown journal, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.31390/gradschool\_dissertations.5640, doi:10.31390/gradschool\_dissertations.5640.

The excerpt does not identify the base material of the LSU processing chamber itself. It describes an existing chamber donated by the LSU Chemistry Department, with a 16 × 16 × 20 inch frame, 16 × 16 × 0.5 inch doors, five doors overall, and a 14-inch-diameter blocking flange at the bottom. The chamber was sealed using ISO-KF clamp connections and a top assembly consisting of a center ring, viewport, and flange; rubber O-rings sealed the doors. Several parts were made in-house: the custom flange was welded and machined at the LSU machine shop, and the scan-head adaptor was a 1/4-inch aluminum plate. Other components, including the center ring, viewport, scan head, F-theta lens, and collimator, were purchased from outside suppliers, while the chamber itself was donated rather than outsourced for fabrication. Practical challenges included adapting an existing chamber, accommodating multiple doors and side-mounted equipment, and achieving reliable vacuum sealing. During operation, the chamber required thorough cleaning when changing powders, rail lubrication with WD40, careful leveling of the build platform, scan-pattern alignment, door bolting, evacuation below 150 Pa, and backfilling with protective gas while maintaining slight positive pressure.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'wen2021lasersurfacetreatment pages 27-33'.

Haifang Wen. Laser surface treatment and laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing study using custom designed 3d printer and the application of machine learning in materials science. Unknown journal, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.31390/gradschool\_dissertations.5640, doi:10.31390/gradschool\_dissertations.5640.

This excerpt does not specify what material the LSU custom LPBF printer chamber itself was made from, how the chamber was machined, or whether its fabrication was performed in-house or outsourced. It does, however, describe a significant practical problem encountered during operation and the resulting design modification. The original processing-chamber design used a gate valve connecting the scan head to the chamber top wall. After several printing cycles, the laser lost power shortly after activation, and the powder could not be fully melted. Investigation showed that fine metal powder had accumulated on the scan-head mirrors, reducing their reflectivity and causing absorption, coating deflection, and thermal lensing. The powder entered through the fine screw used to attach the F-theta lens. The author addressed this by replacing the gate valve with a viewing port made from 2 mm thick 7056 glass, separating the scan head from the printer’s processing chamber. This simplified operation by eliminating the need to open and close the gate valve during printing, but reduced laser power by approximately 10% because of the glass transmission efficiency. Details about chamber construction, machining methods, and fabrication responsibility would need to be obtained from other sections of the dissertation, especially the earlier machine-design sections.

These estimates exclude the additional labor or bonding required to stack and assemble the seven layers. The text identifies setup and programming amortization, process efficiency, labor and machine utilization, and material efficiency as drivers of volume cost reductions. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Part category | Decision | Recommended route | ROM cost comparison, qty. 1–3 | Key controls and rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6061-T651 through-frame chamber, 312 × 222 × 140 mm | **HYBRID: BUY roughing; MAKE finish** | Buy 5.5-in plate with the core waterjet-cut or bandsawn, leaving 3–6 mm machining allowance; stress-relieve/rest; finish-machine datum faces, bore, ports, and interfaces on the VF-4 using multiple qualified setups. Quote a local large-part shop as a schedule fallback. | **Hybrid:** roughly **$1,500–$3,500** including plate and rough cutting, plus about **25–50 internal hours**. **Turnkey online/job shop:** roughly **$4,000–$10,000+**, driven by material removal, several setups, inspection, and shipping. These are planning ranges, not live quotations. | The 312 mm length fits the VF-4 travel, but the 140 mm depth and R10 internal corners require long-reach tooling and careful setup control. Rough cutting avoids converting most of an expensive plate into chips. Machine opposing sealing/datum faces from a common datum scheme and inspect after unclamping. LSU successfully CNC-machined a solid-aluminum LPBF powder chamber in its university shop, but alignment and assembly adjustment remained important (pqac-00000029). |
| 20 mm 6061 floor plate and lid with Parker face glands | **MAKE** | Buy blanks waterjet- or saw-cut; face both sides, drill/ream locating features, and machine each O-ring gland and its mating datum in one final setup on the VF-4. Outsource only blanchard/grind/lap correction if flatness is missed. | **In-house:** approximately **$300–$900 material/blank cutting + 12–25 hours** for the pair. **Outsource:** approximately **$1,500–$4,000** for the pair with drawing-based inspection; online prices rise sharply when flatness, Ra, and reports are added. | These parts establish the chamber seal and tolerance stack, so retaining control and enabling local rework outweighs nominal quote savings. Specify static sealing surfaces at **Ra ≤1.6 µm**, no radial scratches or spiral tool marks, and explicit flatness; published static O-ring guidance permits Ra 1.6 µm but rejects scratches, pits, and spiral scores (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). |
| Door | **MAKE**, unless it is a welded/windowed fabrication | Machine a waterjet-cut 6061 plate in-house; finish the hinge/latch datums and sealing face after all major material removal. If the door contains a welded viewport or complex sheet construction, buy the weldment and finish-machine the seal face in-house. | **In-house solid plate:** about **$250–$800 + 6–15 hours**. **Turnkey outsourced:** about **$700–$2,000**, excluding costly vacuum viewports. | Keep hinge, latch, and seal compression in one datum chain; use hard stops so the hinge does not define final O-ring squeeze. LSU adapted an existing chamber with O-ring-sealed doors and required careful bolting, evacuation, and backfilling during operation (pqac-00000030). |
| 316L build cylinders, 25.4/50.8/76.2 mm H7 bores, 3 mm walls, welded flanges | **BUY specialty finished cylinders** | Obtain 316L seamless tubing with extra wall or near-size precision tubing; have a hydraulic-cylinder/honing specialist weld or receive welded flange assemblies, then finish-bore/hone **after welding** to H7, roundness, straightness, and surface-finish requirements. Ask for a separate quote using stocked honed tube, but verify alloy, wall, and dimensional availability. | **Specialist finished pieces:** roughly **$600–$1,800 each** or **$2,000–$5,000 per three-size set**. Purchasing a suitable stocked honed tube can be cheaper, but short-length 316L exact-ID/H7 material may carry minimum-order and cut charges. Buying a honing machine is unjustified for three pieces; attempting H7 with boring alone creates high scrap/rework risk. | Do not accept ordinary DOM as automatically H7 or vacuum-clean 316L. Welding a 3 mm wall to a flange can distort the bore, so honing before welding is unsafe unless generous post-weld correction is planned. Require actual bore map, cylindricity/straightness, Ra, alloy heat certification, weld procedure, pickling/passivation, and final cleaning. |
| 6061 heater blocks and plates | **MAKE** | Saw or waterjet blanks; machine heater bores, thermocouple holes, pockets, and mounting datums on the VF-4. Use the HRT210 where radial holes reduce setups. | **In-house:** typically **$50–$250 material + 2–8 hours each**. **Online:** commonly **$250–$900 each** at qty. 1 because programming and setup dominate. A university comparison found an internally produced aluminum part at about **$108** versus approximately **$305–$624** from external platforms (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). | Excellent fit for available equipment, and dimensions may change during thermal testing. Ream only interfaces that need close fits; avoid imposing unnecessary tolerances on heater-cartridge holes. |
| Macor standoff rings | **BUY machined**, or buy stock and make only with proper ceramic controls | Send to a machinable-ceramic specialist or precision job shop experienced with Macor; alternatively, turn simple rings on the campus lathe using dedicated carbide tools, dust extraction, light cuts, and inspection. | **Outsource:** about **$100–$400 per ring**, with batch savings for identical rings. **In-house:** low raw-material cost but potentially expensive tool wear, breakage, contamination control, and student/shop time. | Macor is machinable but brittle and dust-generating; edge chipping and thin-ring fracture make ordinary online CNC fulfillment risky. Specify allowable chips, concentricity, flatness, cleaning, and packaging. Keep ceramic dust away from precision machine ways and metal-powder areas. |
| 304 sheet-metal hoppers | **BUY** | Use a domestic laser/waterjet-and-brake sheet-metal vendor; order flat-pattern laser cuts plus bends, then TIG-weld only seams that truly require sealing. Prefer tab-and-slot self-fixturing and standard bend radii. | **Outsource:** approximately **$150–$600 each** or **$400–$1,500 per small set**, depending on bends and welding. In-house fabrication consumes substantial layout, cutting, fixturing, and finishing time without a laser or press brake. | Provide formed-part drawing, flat pattern, grain direction where relevant, bend-radius/K-factor assumptions, weld symbols, and powder-safe edge requirements. Laser-cut sheet parts are a better fit for specialized sheet platforms than general CNC marketplaces. |
| 1.6 mm 5052 laser guard | **BUY** | Order laser-cut and brake-formed 5052-H32 from a sheet-metal platform such as SendCutSend or OSH Cut; install certified interlock hardware and any viewing window separately. | Commonly **$100–$500** for a small formed guard, versus many campus hours for manual cutting and bending. | Use 5052 rather than 6061 for tight bends; specify bend direction/radius, hemmed or deburred edges, enclosure overlaps, hardware, grounding, interlocks, and the applicable laser-safety review. Do not treat a dimensional enclosure quote as certification of laser containment. |
| 316L plenums | **BUY weldment; MAKE final interfaces if needed** | Have a qualified stainless sheet-metal shop laser-cut, form, and TIG-weld the plenums; request back-purged welds where the interior matters. Finish-machine gasket faces, flange datums, or critical adapter bores on campus after welding. | **Fabricated plenums:** roughly **$500–$2,000 each** depending on size, ports, weld length, and leak-test scope. Outsourcing the near-net weldment avoids extensive campus fixturing; in-house finish machining preserves interface control. | Weld distortion can defeat flange flatness, so leak-test and inspect after welding, then machine sealing interfaces. Require 316L traceability, internal weld acceptance, removal of heat tint, passivation, cleanliness, and a stated helium- or pressure-decay leak criterion. LPBF studies show that nonuniform chamber flow creates stagnant regions and process variability, so plenum geometry and final assembly alignment matter (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022). |
| Brackets and adapter rings | **MAKE** | Mill brackets from saw/waterjet blanks on the VF-4; turn concentric adapter rings on the CNC lathe, adding cross-holes on the HRT210 where useful. Buy commodity KF/ISO/CF adapters rather than reproducing standards. | **In-house:** commonly **$20–$150 material + 1–5 hours per part**. **Online:** often **$150–$600 per unique part** at qty. 1–3. Setup and programming amortization drives steep quantity-one prices (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034). | These are ideal training and iteration parts, and local manufacture shortens rework loops. Group parts by stock size and tooling, use common datums, and standardize hole/thread families. Buy standardized vacuum interfaces because catalog geometry, sealing finish, and leak performance are worth more than small material savings. |


*Table: Recommended sourcing route for each custom LPBF-machine part family, matched to the campus equipment and the absence of honing capability. Cost figures are rough-order planning ranges; critical sealing, bore, weld, and inspection requirements should be placed explicitly on drawings and purchase orders.*

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of typical US shop rates for different manufacturing processes in 2024-2026. Include columns for: Process, Academic/University Shop Rate (subsidized), Commercial US Job Shop Rate, Online Platform Effective Rate, and Notes. Processes to include: 3-axis CNC milling, 4/5-axis CNC milling, CNC turning, Waterjet cutting, Laser cutting (sheet metal), TIG welding (steel/aluminum), Wire EDM, Honing (ID/OD), Anodizing (Type II/III), Passivation (316L), Blanchard grinding. Note that academic literature rarely reports explicit hourly rates; use the evidence from FSAE comparison (in-house $108 vs outsource $305-$624) and industry benchmarks. Mark which rates are from literature citations versus industry planning estimates."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Process | Academic/university shop rate, subsidized | Commercial US job-shop rate | Online-platform effective rate | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 3-axis CNC milling | **$35–75/h** | **$75–150/h** | **$100–225/h equivalent** | Planning estimates. At qty. 1–3, setup, CAM, inspection, and platform margin make an hourly conversion imprecise. A documented university case cost about **$108 internally** versus **$305–490 through Xometry, $318–326 through Fictiv, and $572–624 through Protolabs** for an aluminum upright (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). |
| 4/5-axis CNC milling | **$60–120/h** | **$125–250/h** | **$175–350/h equivalent** | Planning estimates. Complex fixtures, probing, collision risk, and scarce capacity raise rates; unusual tool access and fixtures can materially increase price and compromise manufacturability (pqac-00000003). The lab's indexed HRT210 work is normally closer to upper-end 3-axis than simultaneous 5-axis pricing. |
| CNC turning | **$35–70/h** | **$70–140/h** | **$90–200/h equivalent** | Planning estimates. Simple rings and adapters favor in-house turning; live tooling, tight runout, deep bores, certificates, and inspection increase outsourced cost. Online quotations vary because suppliers assign setup and cycle costs differently (pqac-00000034). |
| Waterjet cutting | **$100–175/h machine time**, often **$50–150 minimum** | **$125–250/h**, often **$100–300 minimum** | Usually priced by geometry: **$75–300 minimum/order** | Planning estimates. Best used to remove the chamber-frame core or rough blanks while leaving machining allowance. Pierce count, abrasive consumption, thickness, taper, programming, and material handling dominate—not merely cutting minutes. |
| Laser cutting, sheet metal | **$75–150/h**, if campus equipment exists | **$100–225/h**, often **$75–250 minimum** | Geometry-based; commonly **$30–200 flat** or **$75–500 formed part** | Planning estimates. Online sheet specialists amortize nesting efficiently; suitable for guards, hoppers, and plenum panels. Laser-edge and bend tolerances do not establish gasket-face flatness, vacuum cleanliness, or leak tightness. |
| TIG welding, steel/aluminum | **$40–90/h** | **$90–175/h** | Rarely transparent; approximately **$125–250/h equivalent** in fabricated-part quotes | Planning estimates. Stainless back-purging, aluminum cleaning, fixturing, distortion control, weld documentation, and leak testing add cost. Finish-machine critical faces after welding. LSU's custom LPBF build used a flange welded and machined by its university shop (pqac-00000030). |
| Wire EDM | **$50–100/h** | **$100–225/h** | **$150–300/h equivalent**, often manual quote | Planning estimates. Start holes, skim passes, wire consumption, unattended burn time, inspection, and minimum charges matter. Reserve for geometries or hardened materials that cannot be milled economically—not routine brackets. |
| Honing, ID/OD | **$60–125/h** where available | **$100–225/h**, commonly **$250–750 minimum/job** | Generally manual quote; **$150–300/h equivalent** | Planning estimates. Tooling/mandrel size, stock removal, bore length, cylindricity, and measurement drive cost. Because this lab lacks honing, H7 build cylinders should go to a specialist; final honing should ordinarily follow flange welding to remove weld distortion. |
| Anodizing, Type II | Usually outside service; **$75–200 lot charge** | **$100–300 minimum lot**, then roughly **$20–100/part** | **$75–250 minimum/order** when platform-offered | Planning estimates. Masking, color matching, sealing, rack marks, dimensional growth, stripping/rework, and certification add cost. Keep O-ring faces and precision fits masked if coating thickness is not included in the tolerance. |
| Anodizing, Type III hardcoat | Usually outside service; **$150–350 lot charge** | **$200–500 minimum lot**, then roughly **$40–175/part** | **$150–400 minimum/order** when available | Planning estimates. Greater dimensional change and process variability than Type II; specify thickness, masking, sealing, and post-coating dimensions. Avoid coating vacuum-sealing faces unless explicitly designed and qualified. |
| Passivation, 316L | Usually outside service; **$100–250 lot charge** | **$150–400 minimum lot**, then roughly **$20–100/part** | **$100–350/order** when available | Planning estimates. Specify **ASTM A967/A967M** or **AMS 2700**, method, certificate, and final rinse/dry/packaging. Passivation is not electropolishing or vacuum cleaning; welded parts normally need heat-tint removal/pickling first. |
| Blanchard grinding | **$60–110/h** where available | **$100–200/h**, often **$200–500 minimum** | Usually manual quote; **$125–250/h equivalent** | Planning estimates. Useful for rapid correction of plate parallelism/flatness, but its rotary lay is not automatically suitable for an O-ring track; finish-machine or lap the actual sealing band as required. Static O-ring guidance permits approximately **Ra 1.6 µm** but rejects scratches, pits, concentric marks, and spiral scores (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). |
| Interpretation of ranges | Academic shops often charge only direct labor/material or subsidized internal rates | Commercial rates include labor, machine ownership, overhead, tooling, QA, and profit | Platform prices bundle setup, programming, machine time, network/platform margin, QA, and sometimes freight | Except for the explicitly cited part quotations, these are **2024–2026 budgetary planning estimates**, not published tariff schedules or live quotes. Academic literature rarely reports explicit hourly rates; current released CAD, drawings, quantities, documentation, and a common inspection package should be quoted by at least three suppliers. Time-driven costing literature confirms that machine/activity duration and capacity rate are core drivers, while actual quotations also depend on batching, tooling already installed, remnants, and supplier allocation of setup versus cycle cost (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000038). |


*Table: Budgetary 2024–2026 US rates for campus shops, commercial job shops, and online manufacturing platforms. Most figures are marked as planning estimates because published academic sources generally report complete part quotations rather than hourly tariffs.*

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended

Search for patents to increase the patent count.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

A JSON string representing the updated objective.

- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.

filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Please give sourced advice on make-versus-buy and outsourcing for the custom parts of a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion machine, built by a US university lab that has a Haas VF-4 3-axis mill with an HRT210 4th axis, a CNC lathe, TIG welding and wire EDM in campus shops, and no honing machine. The custom parts are about 48 machined parts: a 6061-T651 through-frame chamber (312 x 222 x 140 mm outside, 16 mm walls, R10 inside corners, cut from 5.5 in. plate with the core removed by waterjet or bandsaw), a 20 mm 6061 floor plate and a lid with O-ring face glands (Parker), a door, 316L build cylinders bored and honed to 25.4 / 50.8 / 76.2 mm H7 with 3 mm walls welded to flanges, 6061 heater blocks and plates, Macor standoff rings, 304 sheet-metal hoppers, a 1.6 mm 5052 laser guard, 316L plenums, brackets and adapter rings; about 264 shop hours were estimated, of which 116 h is CAM programming and 99 h setups.

Questions: (1) What do instant-quote platforms (Xometry, Protolabs, SendCutSend, OSH Cut, Fictiv, Protolabs Network/Hubs, JLCCNC, PCBWay, RapidDirect) typically charge for parts like these in quantity 1-3, what lead times, and what are known pitfalls when ordering vacuum-sealing parts from them (O-ring gland surface finish Ra 0.8-1.6 um, flatness, tapped holes into blind pockets, helical inserts, material certs, passivation of 316L, cleanliness for vacuum)? (2) Which parts should a lab make itself and which should it buy (sheet metal by laser/waterjet with bending, turned parts, the large frame, the honed tubes)? Is it cheaper to buy a precision honed or DOM tube (or a ground-and-honed hydraulic cylinder tube) than to hone in-house or by a job shop? (3) Are there vendors who sell standard vacuum chambers or blank chamber bodies (Kurt J. Lesker, Ideal Vacuum, MDC, Nor-Cal, LewVac) that could replace a custom-machined chamber at this size, and their typical prices? (4) Typical shop rates for academic and job shops (CNC milling, turning, waterjet, TIG welding, wire EDM, honing, anodize/passivation) in the US in 2025-2026. (5) What are lessons from labs that built custom LPBF or other vacuum/inert-gas chambers about outsourcing (tolerance stack-ups, leak testing, re-work)? Please give numbers with sources.

<jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Purpose</jats:title><jats:p>Cloud Manufacturing (CM) is the manufacturing version of Cloud Computing and aims to increase flexibility in the provision of manufacturing services. On-demand manufacturing services can be requested by users to the cloud and this enables the concept of Manufacturing-as-a-Service (MaaS). Given the considerable number of prototypes and proofs of concept addressed in literature, this work seeks real CM platforms to study them from a business perspective, in order to discover what MaaS concretely means today and how these platforms are operating.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Design/methodology/approach</jats:title><jats:p>Since the number of real applications of this paradigm is very limited (if the authors exclude prototypes), the research approach is qualitative. It is based on empirical data and inductively researches differences among them (e.g. stakeholders, operational flows, capabilities offered and scalability level).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title content-type="abstract-subheading">Findings</jats:title><jats:p>MaaS has come true in some contexts, and today it is following two different deployment models: open or closed to the provider side. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Manufacturing-as-a-Service (MaaS) model has been proposed by the research community and has been given significant attention by the industry as it holds the promise for agility and resilience of production networks. However, there are significant challenges (such as unforeseen events) that should be overcome for successful implementation of the MaaS model. The objective of this work is to enable companies to mitigate both short- and medium-term unforeseen events and to support them to participate in a dynamic MaaS network. To address these needs, five research objectives are suggested and discussed: 1) actionable propositions for adapting supply chains or internal production; 2) dynamic supply chain generation; 3) building trust in MaaS networks; 4) dynamic planning and scheduling of production processes; 5) dynamic assembly and disassembly. Moreover, a novel digital platform for implementing and integrating these objectives is presented. This paper presents the architectural foundations and methodological framework; empirical validation through two industrial pilots—one from the automotive domain (Continental, CZ) and one from the bicycle industry (Aska, BE)—is ongoing, with the validation methodology and target metrics defined herein. The work takes place in the context of the research and innovation action (RIA) project RAASCEMAN (Resilient and Adaptive Supply Chains for Capability-based Manufacturing as a Service Networks), funded by the Horizon Europe program.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>`Atmospheric water generation (AWG) offers a sustainable solution to global freshwater scarcity by extracting moisture from the air. Transitioning from flat 2D plates to three-dimensional triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) geometries substantially increases available surface area and, in turn, the potential water generation rate. This shift enhances condensation efficiency, as 3D structures expose more surface within the same volume, maximizing contact with humid air. While additive manufacturing (AM) enables the creation of these intricate TPMS structures, AM processes are often constrained by limited material selection, suboptimal surface roughness, and high unit costs that hinder economical scalability. To address these limitations, this study explores whether subtractive manufacturing can serve as a viable and scalable alternative for producing TPMS geometries with greater material flexibility and improved surface finish. To overcome these challenges, this study investigates the feasibility of employing multi-axis subtractive manufacturing—specifically computer numerical control (CNC) machining—to fabricate a range of common TPMS topologies (Gyroid, Schwarz, Diamond, Lidinoid, Neovius, and Split-P). Aluminum 6061-T6 is used for its thermal conductivity, machinability, and corrosion resistance. Two machining strategies, unit-cell and layer-by-layer approaches, are developed using CAD preprocessing and toolpath optimization to address issues of tool accessibility, collision avoidance, and surface fidelity. Experimental results demonstrate successful fabrication of Schwarz and Neovius single-layer structures with acceptable dimensional accuracy and surface finish, while more complex geometries encountered limitations due to tool reach and excessive machining time. A detailed cost comparison reveals that, for medium to high production volumes, subtractive methods can reduce per-part cost by up to 75% compared to direct metal laser sintering (DMLS)-based AM, making CNC machining a compelling alternative for scalable deployment of TPMS-enhanced AWG components. Finally, the paper outlines the key technical hurdles—such as fixture design and cutter selection—that must be addressed to broaden the applicability of subtractive manufacturing for future AWG system development.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Precision manufacturing requirements are the key to ensuring the quality and reliability of biomedical implants. The powder bed fusion (PBF) technique offers a promising solution, enabling the creation of complex, patient-specific implants with a high degree of precision. This technology is revolutionizing the biomedical industry, paving the way for a new era of personalized medicine. This review explores and details powder bed fusion 3D printing and its application in the biomedical field. It begins with an introduction to the powder bed fusion 3D-printing technology and its various classifications. Later, it analyzes the numerous fields in which powder bed fusion 3D printing has been successfully deployed where precision components are required, including the fabrication of personalized implants and scaffolds for tissue engineering. This review also discusses the potential advantages and limitations for using the powder bed fusion 3D-printing technology in terms of precision, customization, and cost effectiveness. In addition, it highlights the current challenges and prospects of the powder bed fusion 3D-printing technology. This work offers valuable insights for researchers engaged in the field, aiming to contribute to the advancement of the powder bed fusion 3D-printing technology in the context of precision manufacturing for biomedical applications.

Abstract:

 The goal of this work is to quantify the link between the design features (geometry), in-situ process sensor signatures, and build quality of parts made using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing (AM) process. This knowledge is critical for establishing design rules for AM parts, and to detecting impending build failures using in-process sensor data. As a step towards this goal, the objectives of this work are two-fold:
 1) Quantify the effect of the geometry and orientation on the build quality of thin-wall features. To explain further, the geometry-related factor is the ratio of the length of a thin-wall (l) to its thickness (t) defined as the aspect ratio (length-to-thickness ratio, l/t), and the angular orientation (θ) of the part, which is defined as the angle of the part in the X-Y plane relative to the re-coater blade of the LPBF machine.
 2) Assess the thin-wall build quality by analyzing images of the part obtained at each layer from an in-situ optical camera using a convolutional neural network.
 To realize these objectives, we designed a test part with a set of thin-wall features (fins) with varying aspect ratio from Titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) material — the aspect ratio l/t of the thin-walls ranges from 36 to 183 (11 mm long (constant), and 0.06 mm to 0.3 mm in thickness). These thin-wall test parts were built under three angular orientations of 0°, 60°, and 90°. Further, the parts were examined offline using X-ray computed tomography (XCT). Through the offline XCT data, the build quality of the thin-wall features in terms of their geometric integrity is quantified as a function of the aspect ratio and orientation angle, which suggests a set of design guidelines for building thin-wall structures with LPBF. To monitor the quality of the thin-wall, in-process images of the top surface of the powder bed were acquired at each layer during the build process. The optical images are correlated with the post build quantitative measurements of the thin-wall through a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN). The statistical correlation (Pearson coefficient, ρ) between the offline XCT measured thin-wall quality, and CNN predicted measurement ranges from 80% to 98%. Consequently, the impending poor quality of a thin-wall is captured from in-situ process data.

Abstract:
This article aims to highlight the development of an intermittent controller designed to compensate and rectify the lack of fusion (LoF) zones that are induced during the LPBF process. The initial step involved the usage of the self-organizing map (SOM) algorithm to identify the location of LoF defects. Subsequently, the identified defects undergo clustering through the K-means algorithm to form a matrix of cells on the build plate. The center of each cell that encompasses the defective area is then selected as the optimal position for increasing laser power during the subsequence printed layer. To identify the optimum laser power value, various artificial voids, mimicking actual defects, are embedded in the coupons. The capping layer that closes the artificial void is then fabricated with different laser powers to heal the underlying defects. Based on the optimum laser power and defect size, several controlling rules are defined to change the laser power in situ in the targeted cells located within the capping layer of defects. The change in laser power is transferred as a laser correction file (LCF) to the actuator via the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) broker. Finally, the performance of the controller is evaluated by designing and fabricating two new sets of experiments, including artificial and randomized defects. The results are validated by performing a micro CT scan, in which the density of defects is analyzed on parts produced with and without the controller. The results suggest that the use of the controller increased the density of the sample with randomized defects by up to 1%.

Abstract:
Abstract Operational research is a significant part of management, based on improving efficiency, operability, and machine quality. Those improvements influence the time of the repair process, workforce availability for the repair process, safety, and environment. The main goal of this article is to investigate the optimal – operating service life of the machine and the optimal – operating time interval for the renewal of the CNC metalworking machine. The research was implemented in a small enterprise in Slovakia that needed a CNC machine in the production process. The research hypothesis was determined H1: Using quantitative models of operational research can manage the machine’s life cycle. We used quantitative mathematical models of operational research. By calculation, we found that the optimal – operational lifetime of the CNC machine is 6 years. The renewal time of the machine is between the 5th and 6th year of use with a minimal level of the total costs for repairs and maintenance. This simulation is essential information for the financial plan for CNC machine renewal. The results of the research showed a confirmed hypothesis. The suggested proactive model is a viable instrument for the machine park in small enterprises with various orientations.

Abstract:
In the context of growing environmental concerns and the demand for more sustainable manufacturing practices, this study evaluates the environmental and economic performance of two production routes for a stainless steel support block used in steel mills. A comparative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) and Life Cycle Costing (LCC) were conducted to assess a conventional subtractive manufacturing process based on Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining versus a hybrid approach that combines Plasma Arc-Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (PA-WAAM) with CNC finishing. The LCA was carried out using ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint and Endpoint methodologies in SimaPro, while the LCC employed a cradle-to-gate cost model. Results showed that the hybrid WAAM-CNC route reduced average environmental impacts by 49% across 18 categories and decreased steel consumption by approximately 70% due to near-net-shape fabrication. Although the hybrid method incurred an approximate 3.5 times increase in unit production cost, this was primarily attributed to equipment investment. In contrast, operational costs such as labor, materials, and consumables were significantly lower—by 66%, 28%, and 45%, respectively. These findings support the hybrid approach as a more sustainable manufacturing alternative with the potential for long-term cost optimization as additive technologies mature.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Accurate project cost estimation remains a major quantitative challenge in technology-intensive engineering programs because expenditure is influenced by interacting technical, procurement, contractual, supplier, schedule, organizational, and financial conditions. This study evaluated machine-learning-assisted project cost estimation and compared conventional statistical approaches with nonlinear predictive models using a retrospective quantitative longitudinal design. The final analytical dataset comprised 1,386 engineering projects from 45 organizations, including 5,126 contracts, 3,964 suppliers, 89,438 purchase orders, 651,720 financial and procurement transactions, and 281,536 engineering records. Analytical data completeness reached 98.6%, while financial reconciliation accuracy reached 99.1%. Mean baseline budget was $18.42 million compared with mean final project cost of $21.08 million, while baseline cost deviation averaged 14.4% and absolute percentage estimation error reached 16.8%. Procurement expenditure demonstrated the strongest correlation with final cost (r = .79), followed by engineering hours (r = .72) and technological complexity (r = .64), while the multivariable model explained 76.8% of final-cost variation. Conventional regression and machine-learning models were evaluated using repeated cross-validation and independent holdout testing. Elastic net represented the strongest conventional benchmark with R² = .789 and MAPE = 10.8%. XGBoost achieved the strongest overall holdout performance with R² = .921, MAE = $1.24 million, RMSE = $1.81 million, and MAPE = 5.9%, corresponding to reductions of 46.3% in MAE, 43.3% in RMSE, and 45.4% in MAPE relative to elastic net. LightGBM and CatBoost produced similarly strong performance. Explainability analysis identified procurement expenditure, engineering hours, technological complexity, cumulative expenditure, and schedule variance as the dominant predictors. Subgroup MAPE ranged from 4.8% to 7.3%, while cross-organizational validation achieved R² = .887 and MAPE = 7.1%. Inferential comparisons produced large overall model effects, with partial eta-squared exceeding .84. The findings demonstrated that integrated, explainable machine-learning models substantially improved the accuracy, stability, and generalizability of project cost estimation across heterogeneous technology-intensive engineering programs.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) is positioned at a pivotal moment, where its long-promised advantages, e.g., lower cost, reduced environmental burden, and accelerated production, are increasingly tangible yet unevenly realized across industries and regions. This review synthesizes evidence from AM processes for different materials to clarify the technical and economic levers that drive outcomes. Cost performance is shown to depend strongly on design choices, deposition rate, post-processing requirements, and feedstock pricing. Environmental impacts hinge on material production routes, regional energy mix, build utilization, and the extent of material reuse. Lead-time reductions are most significant when components are redesigned for AM, when high-throughput processes are applied to compatible geometries, and when production is geographically localized. Emerging digital tools including machine learning, in situ monitoring, and digital twins are accelerating process stabilization and shortening qualification cycles, while hybrid manufacturing lines demonstrate the value of integrating near-net-shape printing with precision finishing. Drawing from these insights, a pragmatic roadmap is proposed: align parts and supply chains with the most suitable AM processes, decarbonize and streamline feedstock production, and increase system utilization. When these conditions are met, AM can deliver broad, quantifiable improvements in cost efficiency, sustainability, and global adoption. By consolidating fragmented evidence into a unified framework, this review responds to the growing need for clarity as AM moves toward broader industrial deployment.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study has addressed the problem of limited transparency in artificial intelligence-supported supplier assessment, where complex predictive models may identify cost risks and recommend sourcing actions without sufficiently explaining the factors responsible for those outputs. The purpose of the study has been to quantitatively examine how Explainable Artificial Intelligence capabilities are associated with Supplier Cost-Risk and Margin Optimization Performance in global manufacturing supply chains. A quantitative, cross-sectional, case-study-based research design has been employed across selected manufacturing and enterprise supply-chain environments using procurement analytics, supplier evaluation systems, AI-supported decision tools, and advanced digital sourcing platforms. Using purposive sampling, 320 questionnaires have been distributed to procurement, sourcing, supply-chain, purchasing, supplier relationship, financial, operations, and AI or analytics professionals, of which 301 have been returned and 289 have been retained as valid responses, producing a 90.3% usable response rate. The study has examined Explainable Supplier Cost-Risk Identification, AI-Enabled Cost Driver Transparency, Explainable Supplier Risk Prioritization and Decision Support, and Explainable Margin Scenario Analytics as predictors of Supplier Cost-Risk and Margin Optimization Performance. Data have been analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, construct-validity tests, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression. Reliability coefficients have ranged from .84 to .91, with KMO = .89 and Bartlett’s Test significant at p < .001. Supplier Cost-Risk and Margin Optimization Performance has recorded M = 4.18, SD = 0.53. All four predictors have demonstrated significant positive correlations with performance, led by Explainable Supplier Cost-Risk Identification, r = .75, followed by AI-Enabled Cost Driver Transparency, r = .72, Explainable Supplier Risk Prioritization and Decision Support, r = .69, and Explainable Margin Scenario Analytics, r = .66, all p < .001. The regression model has explained 71.2% of performance variance, R² = .712, adjusted R² = .708, F (4, 284) = 175.50, p < .001, with significant standardized effects of β = .31, .28, .24, and .21, respectively. These findings indicate that explainable AI can strengthen supplier cost visibility, risk prioritization, sourcing decision quality, and margin-oriented management by making AI-supported assessments more interpretable and managerially actionable.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Companies are increasingly turning to additive manufacturing as the demand for one-off 3D-printed metal parts rises. The differences in available additive manufacturing technologies necessitate considering both cost and externalities to select the most suitable alternative. This study compares some of the most prevalent metal additive manufacturing technologies through a shop floor-level operational analysis. A steel robotic gripper is considered as a case study, based on which of the complex, interconnected operational factors that influence costs over time are analyzed. The developed cost model facilitates the estimation of costs, identification of cost drivers, and analysis of the impact of various operations management decisions on overall costs. We found that cost performance across Powder-Bed Fusion (PBF), Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM), and CNC machining is determined by part design, quantity, and machine utilization. Although producing parts with complex internal features favors additive manufacturing, CNC outperforms in terms of economy of scale. While PBF offers excellent design freedom and parallel production, it incurs high fixed costs per build in under-utilized situations. A rough but fast method, such as Directed-Energy Deposition (DED)-based additive manufacturing, is believed to be more cost-efficient for large, simple shapes, but is not suitable when fine details are required. Laser-based DED approaches address this limitation of WAAM.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This paper delves into the impacts of an ongoing global crisis on the resilience of supply chains. Furthermore, it proposes measures to address and mitigate the disruptions caused by the prevailing uncertainties. For example, while the economy has started to recover after the pandemic and demand has increased, companies have not fully returned to their pre-pandemic levels. To enhance their supply chain resilience and effectively manage disruptions, one viable strategy is the implementation of flexible/hybrid manufacturing systems. This research is motivated by the specific requirements of Vestel Electronics, a household appliances company, which seeks a flexible/hybrid manufacturing production setup involving dedicated machinery to meet regular demand and the utilisation of flexible manufacturing system (FMS) to handle surges in demand. We employ a scenario-based approach to model demand uncertainty, enabling the company to make immediate and adaptive decisions that take advantage of the cost-effectiveness of standard production and the responsiveness of FMS. To solve the problem, we propose a heuristic algorithm based on column generation. The numerical results demonstrate that our optimisation model provides solutions with an average optimality gap of less than 6% while also reducing the average cost of standard production schemes without FMS by over 12%.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on the design of pressure-resistant seals for underwater observation devices operating in seawater environments. The unique challenges posed by seawater, including its high salinity and corrosive elements, necessitate innovative material selection and precise engineering techniques to ensure the durability and efficiency of the seals. This research focuses on identifying corrosion-resistant elastomers and coatings suitable for withstanding high pressures and temperature fluctuations in the harsh marine environment. Additionally, the study delves into the impact of meticulous assembly practices on the long-term performance and reliability of the sealing components. The research team calculated and designed a prototype of the underwater observation device's shell and successfully conducted a water pressure test at a depth of up to 80 meters. The sealing limit primarily depends on the mechanical properties of the gasket material. When using metal gaskets, the sealing limit can reach up to 5000 psi, equivalent to a depth of 3400 meters, which is also the current testing equipment limit.

Abstract:
Laser-based powder bed fusion is an additive manufacturing process in which a high-power laser melts a thin layer of metal powder layer by layer to yield a three-dimensional object. An inert gas must remove process byproducts formed during laser processing to ensure a stable and consistent process. The process byproducts include a plasma plume and spatter particles. An NC sensor gantry is installed inside a bespoke open-architecture laser-based powder bed fusion system to experimentally characterize the gas velocity throughout the processing area. The flow maps are compared to manufactured samples, where the relative density and melt pools are analyzed, seeking a potential correlation between local gas flow conditions and the components. The results show a correlation between low gas flow velocities and increased porosity, leading to lower part quality. Local flow conditions across the build plate also directly impact components, highlighting the importance of optimizing the gas flow subsystem. The experimental flow analysis method enables optimization of the gas flow inlet geometry, and the data may be used to calibrate the computational modeling of the process.

Abstract:
Although additive manufacturing (AM) is becoming increasingly popular for various applications, few studies have addressed design and potential problems in thin wall fabrication for the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process. In the LPBF process, rapid cooling induces thermal shrinkage, which in turn, results in high residual stress and complicates thin wall fabrication. The minimum wall thickness is limited by the parameters and machine settings while the dimensional accuracy is controlled by the powder size, scan strategy, and part geometry. The ability to fabricate thin-wall components is important for applications such as heat exchangers (HX). This study explores the performance of the LPBF process by fabricating thin walls with extreme geometries in different processing conditions and alloys using an EOS M290 LPBF machine. Results show that the material, part design, and scanning strategy contribute to the variation in thin wall dimensions. A maximum inclination angle of 60° and a minimum wall thickness of ~ 100 μm in Ti-6Al-4V, Inconel 718, and AlSi10Mg were achieved using optimized part design and processing conditions. The effects of part design and material on the thermal distortion and surface finish of thin walls were also investigated leading to a discussion on how the scan mode assigned by the EOS software affects design and fabrication. Additionally, synchrotron-based X-ray micro-tomography (μSXCT) was utilized to quantify the porosity in thin-wall structures and to correlate it with the integrity of the structures. Comprehensive design guidelines presented in this work can increase the success rate of fabricating thin-wall geometries.
