Abstract:
Nowadays the reduction of fuel consumption is the most important challenge for engine development. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) as an additive manufacturing process with its implied design freedom makes it possible to reduce combustion emissions, increase engine efficiency and respond specifically to customer requirements. In this work, the outstanding degree of freedom of LPBF is exploited for a new design concept for a cylinder head of an engine in automotive industry in order to address further reduction of fuel consumption through improved cooling performance. Within the given installation space and under consideration of the existing mounting and connection positions, the design concept was developed, subsequently manufactured and reworked. In order to develop a design that meets the LPBF requirements, both the potential of the LPBF using the geometric degrees of freedom as effectively as possible and the limitations are considered. The opposing design drivers between exploitation of potentials and limitations in LPBF are achieved by an iterative design process supported by an own developed design tool. With the new design concept, a reduction of the metal temperature in the cylinder head of approx. 25 K is achieved, verified by simulation.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Much of the potential of industrial additive manufacturing (AM) is said to lie in the digital specification of components that can be transmitted seamlessly and unambiguously to partners fostering flexible outsourcing. In industry, we observe nuanced AM supply chain governance structures that result from make‐or‐buy decisions, with a tendency to implement AM in‐house. Thus, there is a discrepancy between what is discussed in the literature and implemented in practice. We apply a multiple‐case study approach to investigate <jats:italic>why</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>how</jats:italic> AM impacts the make‐or‐buy decision of manufacturing firms. We identify four decision profiles demonstrating the spectrum of specific governance structures and develop a framework to explain the underlying rationales. We find strong arguments for in‐house AM including firms’ perceived need to protect their digitally encapsulated intellectual property, reevaluation of their core competencies, commitment to internal learning, and senior management's enthusiasm for AM. By using transaction cost economics and the resource‐based view, we contribute to the understanding of how arguments of these general theories are modified by the digital and emerging traits of AM. We reveal contradicting guidance in the theories’ argumentation for the case of AM and provide managers a clear perspective on alternative strategies for their AM implementation process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Purpose: Make-or-buy decisions represent a critical dilemma faced by many firms. The appropriate decision between designing and manufacturing parts or services in-house, buying them from external providers or combining both is a fundamental firm process. This paper seeks to address this question by updating the traditional make-or-buy literature with new academic insights, developing a make-or-buy framework with a tool for its operationalisation to help managers evaluate sourcing decisions.Design/methodology/approach:  First, a literature review of the principal theories and approaches about make-or-buy decisions is discussed. Second, the development of the make-or-buy framework is described and explained based on the results of qualitative interviews with practitioners and a set of interviews of an in-firm case study. Third, the results and the implementation of the framework are outlined.Findings: Our study not only validates the proposed framework through a set of in-firm make-or-buy decisions, but also provides a structure for its implementation and design a decision matrix with a pairwise comparison tool for helping practitioners to put the framework into practice.Research limitations/implications: This paper aims to contribute to the study of the make-or-buy literature in supply chain management through the graphical representation of why and how make-or-buy decisions are made. Interestingly, the paper presents relevant dimensions and factors to be studied and evaluates possible outcomes when approaching make-or-buy decisions.Originality/value: Our results suggest that practitioners should combine this framework with a pairwise comparison matrix and a multi-criteria decision analysis based on the TOPSIS methodology to assess strategic sourcing decisions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study examines a multi-item manufacturing problem with a single machine, an outsourcer, and random defective items. To cope with the increasing multi-product demands from global markets, modern manufacturing firms must make an efficient production plan to satisfy customer’s needs with quality goods and smooth the in-house fabrication schedule and utilization. Outsourcing is an effective option to avoid machine overloads and smooth fabrication schedules. Further, the fabrication of random defective products is inevitable because of unanticipated factors in real manufacturing environments. These products must be identified, separated and discarded to retain the desired quality of the finished lot. To address the above-mentioned concerns, this study develops a mathematical model to represent a hybrid stock refilling system, employs mathematical derivations to find long-run average system expenses, and uses an optimization technique to derive a closed-form common rotation time for this hybrid system. The results of this study show the individual and combined impacts of variations in outsourcing percentages and scrap rates on optimal rotation time and diverse core system parameters (such as machine utilization, specific cost component, etc.) to facilitate planning, controlling, and decision making in such a particular hybrid fabrication system.

About 40% of employment in manufacturing is in services functions. This paper develops a measure of narrow outsourcing: the matching of services functions that are performed by workers who are inside manufacturing firms to the same services functions that are provided by outside suppliers. Narrow outsourcing is entered into labour demand functions where labour is classified by business functions. The impact of narrow offshoring on manufacturing labour demand is small on average but depends strongly on the complexity of the value chain, the policy environment, and ICT maturity. The IT and R&D functions are most sensitive to offshoring.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) is regarded as a technology that has transformative and disruptive potential in nearly all industries. However, AM is not only about new production equipment and processes. Given the decreasing degree of vertical integration in many companies, suppliers add significant value to the finished product. AM might lead to the redesign of production networks, including a scenario in which the buyer uses AM to produce parts with data provided by suppliers. Overall, AM could have a major impact on the ways in which buyers and suppliers collaborate in the future. Nevertheless, research on AM in the field of industrial procurement remains scarce. This is surprising, given that AM is not only changing traditional procurement categories and creating new ones (comprising printers, powder raw materials, data and the associated engineering services) but AM’s widely discussed potential for decentralisation might also restructure the logistical aspects (transport, stocks) of supply chains. In addition, AM may resurrect the old procurement question of ‘make or buy’. Current research focuses on the logistical aspects of AM and concerns such issues of decentralisation (such as the diminishing need for transportation and the design of transport networks). In contrast, this research addresses the question of whether AM demands new answers to strategic sourcing questions. For this purpose, academic journal literature concerning procurement and AM search strings is reviewed. Selected articles are analysed using a fine-grained analytical framework of procurement strategies. The findings show that existing research lacks theoretical approaches and a systematic view of the topic. Specifically, the analysis reveals a number of distinct knowledge gaps, which present several potential directions for future research.

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>O-ring seals are critical to ensuring the reliability of mechanical systems under harsh operating conditions. However, the classical parallel plate leakage model often neglects the effects of surface roughness and radial pressure distribution, leading to insufficient prediction accuracy. This study addresses this limitation by extending the classical parallel plate leakage theory to develop an optimized circular plate gap leakage model for O-rings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A leakage rate correction factor μ 1 is introduced to quantify the effect of surface roughness, establishing an equivalent relationship between the micro-scale rough interface and the ideal smooth surface. The leakage rates of rough surfaces with different roughness levels under various differential pressures are theoretically calculated. Experimental validation is carried out under differential pressures of 0.3 MPa and 0.6 MPa, as well as surface roughness Ra values of 0.8 μm, 1.6 μm, and 3.2 μm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At a differential pressure of 0.4 MPa, the leakage rate reaches 0.67 × 10 −12 m 3 /s when Ra = 3.2μm , which is 1.8 times that of the case with Ra = 0.8μm. Experimental results show that: (1) At the same surface roughness, the cumulative leakage volume increases with the increase of differential pressure; when Ra = 1.6μm, the cumulative leakage volume at 0.6 MPa is approximately 1.5 times that at 0.3 MPa. (2) At the same differential pressure, a larger Ra results in a higher cumulative leakage volume; at 0.3 MPa, the cumulative leakage volume at Ra = 3.2μm is about 1.7 times that at Ra = 0.8μm. Overall, the leakage rate increases almost linearly with the increase of both differential pressure and surface roughness. The relative error between theoretical and experimental values is within 15%.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The relative error within 15% confirms the reliability of the proposed model. However, uncertainties in the model primarily stem from unaccounted factors, including high temperature, long-term O-ring aging, extreme high pressure, and idealized model assumptions. Consequently, the model is only valid under conditions of room temperature, low pressure, and short-term service. Nevertheless, this work provides a robust analytical framework for O-ring leakage prediction and sealing performance optimization in engineering applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
A mechanical face seal is an important component of variety of pumps used in chemical, petrochemical and process industry. The primary function of a mechanical seal is to prevent leakage of the process fluid from the pump housing and shaft to the environment. The factors that affect the performance of a mechanical seal to leak are friction, wear and its thermal characteristics. Improving upon the thermal characteristics of a mating ring in a mechanical seal would enhance its performance. Implanting a heat exchanger in the mating ring hold great promise for improving the performance of mechanical seals from the viewpoint of reducing heat at the interface and hence enhance the performance of the mechanical seal. To reveal what affect the implanted heat exchangers can have on the thermal characteristics of different seals, in this thesis, three different designs of mating rings were tested in a test rig and the results were compared to a conventional seal in this thesis. A new design of a mechanical seal with an implanted heat exchanger in its mating ring is reported. The mating ring incorporates an internal channel in which a coolant (either a gas or a liquid) flows to remove heat from the seal face. Prototypes were built and tested in a pump. Results are indicative of effective cooling and improved performance when compared to a conventional seal. A Coating on the mating ring was successfully implemented. A simplified heat transfer analysis using the results of the finite element method is also presented for all the seal designs.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a transformative route for producing lightweight, high-precision, and geometrically complex components in aerospace, biomedical, and microelectronic sectors. Among AM technologies, Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) offers exceptional design freedom; however, its widespread adoption particularly for titanium alloys remains constrained by two persistent challenges: shrinkage-induced dimensional deviation and porosity-related performance loss. In LPBF-processed Ti-6Al-4V, residual linear deviation typically falls within 0.1–0.8% when geometric compensation, preheating, and support strategies are implemented, while raw, uncompensated shrinkage is more commonly reported in the range of 1.2–2.0%, especially for thin-wall or thermally constrained geometries. Volumetric contraction (approximately 2–6%) may remain significant depending on part architecture and localized thermal accumulation. Concurrently, gas-induced and lack-of-fusion pores continue to undermine fatigue resistance and dimensional reliability. Research into process optimization, thermal management, and post-processing such as Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP), vacuum sintering, and stress-relief annealing has improved density and mechanical integrity, while recent developments in AI-assisted monitoring, physics-informed models, and digital-twin frameworks are redefining defect prediction and control. Drawing on more than 100 peer-reviewed studies, this review synthesizes mechanism-driven insights and outlines a forward-looking roadmap, demonstrating how hybrid processing, real-time sensing, and data-centric control collectively advance the pathway toward defect-minimized, industrial-scale manufacturing of titanium components.</jats:p>

Valid Text Names: 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 1-5', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 5-8', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 8-11', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 11-14', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 14-17', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 17-20', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 20-25', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 25-29', 'gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular pages 29-31' BibTex: @article{gotsch2019anultraflexiblemodular, author = "Götsch, Thomas and Wernig, Eva-Maria and Klötzer, Bernhard and Schachinger, Thomas and Kunze-Liebhäuser, Julia and Penner, Simon", title = "An ultra-flexible modular high vacuum setup for thin film deposition.", year = "2019", journal = "The Review of scientific instruments", volume = "90 2", pages = "023902", month = "Feb", doi = "10.1063/1.5065786", url = "https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5065786", publisher = "AIP Publishing", issue = "2", issn = "0034-6748" } Abstract: A modular high vacuum chamber dedicated to thin film deposition is presented. We detail the vacuum and gas infrastructure required to operate two highly flexible chambers simultaneously, with a focus on evaporation techniques (thermal and electron beam) and magnetron sputtering, including baking equipment to remove residual water from the chamber. The use of O-ring-sealed flat flanges allows a tool-free assembly process, in turn enabling rapid changes of the whole setup. This leads to a high flexibility regarding the deposition techniques as the chamber can be adapted to different sources within minutes, permitting the formation of multilayer systems by consecutive depositions onto the same substrate. The central piece of the chamber is a flat flange ground glass tube or cross. The glass recipient permits optical monitoring of the deposition process. Further equipment, such as for the introduction of gases, additional pressure gauges, or evaporators, can be incorporated via specifically designed stainless steel/aluminum interconnectors and blank flanges. In the end, we demonstrate the preparation of an unsupported thin film system consisting of electron-beam-evaporated platinum nanoparticles embedded in magnetron-sputtered zirconia (ZrO2), deposited onto NaCl single crystals, which subsequently can be removed by dissolution. These films are further analyzed by means of transmission electron microscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and atomic force microscopy. Valid Text Names: 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 1-3', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 3-6', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 6-10', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 10-13', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 13-16', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 16-20', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 20-24', 'elliot2014integratingatomiclayer pages 24-25' BibTex: @article{elliot2014integratingatomiclayer, author = "Elliot, Alan J. and Malek, Gary A. and Lu, Rongtao and Han, Siyuan and Yiu, Haifeng and Zhao, Shiping and Wu, Judy Z.", title = "Integrating atomic layer deposition and ultra-high vacuum physical vapor deposition for in situ fabrication of tunnel junctions.", year = "2014", journal = "The Review of scientific instruments", volume = "85 7", pages = "073904", month = "May", doi = "10.48550/arxiv.1405.1069", url = "https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1405.1069", publisher = "arXiv" } Abstract: Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a promising technique for growing ultrathin, pristine dielectrics on metal substrates, which is essential to many electronic devices. Tunnel junctions are an excellent example which require a leak-free, ultrathin dielectric tunnel barrier of typical thickness around 1 nm between two metal electrodes. A challenge in the development of ultrathin dielectric tunnel barriers using ALD is controlling the nucleation of dielectrics on metals with minimal formation of native oxides at the metal surface for high-quality interfaces between the tunnel barrier and metal electrodes. This poses a critical need for integrating ALD with ultra-high vacuum (UHV) physical vapor deposition. In order to address these challenges, a viscous-flow ALD chamber was designed and interfaced to an UHV magnetron sputtering chamber via a load lock. A sample transportation system was implemented for in situ sample transfer between the ALD, load lock, and sputtering chambers. Using this integrated ALD-UHV sputtering system, superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) Nb-Al/Al2O2/Nb Josephson tunnel junctions were fabricated with tunnel barriers of thickness varied from sub-nm to ~1 nm. The suitability of using an Al wetting layer for initiation of the ALD Al2O3 tunnel barrier was investigated with ellipsometry, atomic force microscopy, and electrical transport measurements. With optimized processing conditions, leak-free SIS tunnel junctions were obtained, demonstrating the viability of this integrated ALD-UHV sputtering system for the fabrication of tunnel junctions and devices comprised of metal-dielectric-metal multilayers. Developing GLAD Parameters to Control the Deposition of Nanostructured Thin Film Valid Text Names: 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 1-2', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 2-5', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 5-7', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 7-10', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 10-13', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 13-16', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 16-17', 'bronicki2022developinggladparameters pages 17-18' BibTex: @article{bronicki2022developinggladparameters, author = "Bronicki, Jakub and Grochala, Dominik and Rydosz, Artur", title = "Developing GLAD Parameters to Control the Deposition of Nanostructured Thin Film", year = "2022", journal = "Sensors", volume = "22", pages = "651", month = "Jan", doi = "10.3390/s22020651", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/s22020651", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "2", issn = "1424-8220" } Abstract: In this paper, we describe the device developed to control the deposition parameters to manage the glancing angle deposition (GLAD) process of metal-oxide thin films for gas-sensing applications. The GLAD technique is based on a set of parameters such as the tilt, rotation, and substrate temperature. All parameters are crucial to control the deposition of nanostructured thin films. Therefore, the developed GLAD controller enables the control of all parameters by the scientist during the deposition. Additionally, commercially available vacuum components were used, including a three-axis manipulator. High-precision readings were tested, where the relative errors calculated using the parameters provided by the manufacturer were 1.5% and 1.9% for left and right directions, respectively. However, thanks to the formula developed by our team, the values were decreased to 0.8% and 0.69%, respectively. The excerpt describes an open-architecture, custom-built high-pressure laser powder bed fusion testbed designed to independently control laser power, scan speed, scan strategy, spot size, inert-gas flow, and ambient pressure. The chamber was a commercially supplied Parr Instrument Company pressure vessel rated to 1900 psig, with a cylindrical 2.5-inch-diameter by 6.5-inch-long bore, multiple ¼-inch NPT ports, and an oblong window flange. Sapphire was selected for the pressure window because of its fracture toughness and infrared transmission. A removable, kinematically constrained build platform enabled repeatable alignment of the powder bed with the laser focal plane. The platform carried the sample plate, while a fused-quartz microscope slide acted as a sacrificial spatter shield. Gas-flow design was a major challenge: the small chamber promoted recirculation and window contamination, so COMSOL simulations evaluated baffles, guide vanes, funneling, outlet enlargement, and a secondary nozzle. The final nozzle was CAD-designed and physically 3D-printed, with testing confirming effective flow across the print area. Abstract:
<jats:p>The automation of loading and unloading operations for CNC vertical milling centers has become increasingly important due to rising production costs, labor shortages, and the pursuit of higher productivity and efficiency. This paper investigates the challenges associated with automating these processes, particularly focusing on optimizing workspace utilization, reducing auxiliary times, and improving overall workflow in CNC production environments. An overview of CNC technology development and its current capabilities is provided, highlighting the essential role of G-code programming and the transition from manual to computer-aided manufacturing. Key issues such as the high cost of programming for small batches, difficulty in recruiting skilled operators, and the economic factors influencing automation decisions are analyzed. The study emphasizes the critical importance of careful investment planning, including return on investment (ROI) considerations, productivity gains, and quality improvements. Practical guidelines for robot selection, end-effector design, and CNC-machine communication integration are proposed, along with a workflow model for automating part handling tasks. An experimental application on a VMC 1000L vertical milling center demonstrates the practical aspects and challenges of implementing an automated loading/unloading system, including necessary machine modifications like door automation. The paper concludes that although automation offers significant benefits, it is not universally applicable; a detailed feasibility study based on batch sizes, product complexity, and financial evaluation is crucial for success. Hybrid approaches combining manual and automated operations are suggested for flexible and cost-effective manufacturing strategies. The study highlights the growing role of intelligent automation as a response to market dynamics, labor trends, and technological advancements in the CNC manufacturing sector.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper reviews computer numerical control wood machining research published between 2020 and 2025, exploring how to choose cutting parameters so that surface quality, energy use, tool wear, and environmental impact are balanced. Wood’s anisotropy, hygroscopicity, and biological variability make it so different, even for the same species or board. Two clear shifts have emerged. Optimization work is moving from one-factor-at-a-time experiments toward multi-objective methods built on neural networks, genetic algorithms, and hybrid artificial intelligence schemes. In parallel, edge computing and predictive maintenance are bringing real-time decision-making down to the machine itself. Two gaps also stand out: few studies test sensors and artificial intelligence models under dusty, high-vibration conditions, and existing digital twins remain static and ignore the internal stresses, knots, and grain irregularities revealed during cutting. The paper closes by arguing for a total-process view of sustainability, optimizing surface quality, dust emissions, auxiliary energy use, and tool life simultaneously.</jats:p>

                                   1.3. The Plume

                            The plasma plume forms in the laser–powder interaction zone, where the laser ionizes
                             the atmosphere. In addition, it contains vaporized metal, which rapidly cools and condenses
                               into nanometer-sized particles (10–150 nm). The vapor plume is ejected at remarkably high
                          speeds proportionate to the laser power, reaching several hundreds of meters per second.

                              Uniformity is key in L-PBF when designing the gas ﬂow. The gas ﬂow should be
                       homogeneous over the entire building surface. This includes a deﬁned orientation of the
                          gas ﬂow and a constant gas ﬂow velocity in all areas [19] where a sufﬁcient gas velocity

                                battle turbulence, where similar requirements apply. A settling duct or chamber with ﬂow
                            conditioners like honeycomb and screens improves the ﬂow. The honeycomb improves
                    ﬂow uniformity by aligning the ﬂow with the axis of the pipe and decreasing larger-scale

Abstract:
<jats:p>Reproducible electrochemical characterization in bench-scale flow cells remains limited by variability in cell architecture, assembly practices, and operating conditions across users and laboratories. Although numerous cell designs have been reported, comprehensive guidance detailing component selection, fabrication, assembly, and testing protocols is largely absent. Here, we present a compact flow cell engineered to improve experimental rigor while maintaining architectural flexibility and cost-effectiveness. The platform incorporates interchangeable components and is amenable to a variety of testing formats, enabling adaptation to diverse electrochemical applications including redox flow batteries, electrolyzers, and fuel cells. The small-scale of the device lowers volume and area requirements for electrolytes and cell components, respectively, facilitating high-throughput, yet systematic studies of emerging chemistries and materials. As a representative use case, we characterize cell performance using two diagnostic configurations and a model redox electrolyte, common in flow battery literature. We also present a framework distinguishing marginal and total repeatability to quantify variability across independent cell builds and operators. Using cell polarization and galvanostatic cycling protocols, we demonstrate consistent performance across configurations and users. By coupling transparent design documentation with a quantitative repeatability framework, this work seeks to establish a reproducible foundation for bench-scale flow cell experimentation and to support cross-laboratory comparability in electrochemical research.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Manufacturing as a Service (MaaS) enables a paradigm shift in the current manufacturing landscape, from integrated production and inflexible, fragile supply chains to open production and flexible, robust supply chains. As part of this evolution, new scaling effects for production capacities and customer segments are possible. This article describes how to accomplish this paradigm shift for the automotive industry by building a digital MaaS ecosystem for the large-scale automotive innovation project Catena-X, which aims at a standardized global data exchange based on European values. A digital MaaS ecosystem can not only achieve scaling effects, but also realize new business models and overcome current and future challenges in the areas of legislation, sustainability, and standardization. This article analyzes the state-of-the-art of MaaS ecosystems and describes the development of a digital MaaS ecosystem based on an updated and advanced version of the reference architecture for smart connected factories, called the Smart Factory Web. Furthermore, this article describes a demonstrator for a federated MaaS marketplace for Catena-X which leverages the full technological potential of this digital ecosystem. In conclusion, the evaluation of the implemented digital ecosystem enables the advancement of the reference architecture Smart Factory Web, which can now be used as a blueprint for open, sustainable, and resilient digital manufacturing ecosystems.

2.5. Electrodes and separators/membranes

   The design choice of stackable gaskets accommodates a wide range of electrode thicknesses, enabling testing of both novel con­
structs and commercial standards. For this flow cell, porous graphitic electrodes, such as carbon papers, felts, and cloths, which can be

                                                                4T.R. Goodwin et al.                                                                                                 HardwareX 28 (2026) e00834

functionalized with catalysts through a variety of methods, are mostly commonly implemented. Metal foams and meshes are also
compatible with this architecture. In addition, the flow cell readily supports small-area, nonstandard electrodes, such as those
fabricated via non-solvent induced phase separation (NIPS) and electrospinning [22,34].
  A wide variety of membranes or separators can be utilized. The membrane or separator is positioned between two gaskets; because
there is no dedicated cavity for this component, sealing is achieved by either (1) compression on the membrane itself such that
electrolyte does not pass through its pores at the gasket-membrane interface or (2) deformation of the gasket stack around the region
not covered by the membrane. Consequently, the maximum usable thickness of the membrane or separator depends on  its
compressibility and that of the gasket to conform around it. In practice, this flow cell accommodates separators and membranes
ranging in thickness from ca. 10 μm to 1 mm, including commercial offerings such as Celgard, Daramic, Nafion, and Fumasep. This
platform is also compatible with bespoke or emerging separators, membranes, and composites (e.g., ceramic composite membranes)
[39,60].

2.6.  Critical balance of plant

   At minimum, the flow cell must be connected to tubing, a pump, an electrolyte reservoir, and a potentiostat. While there are many
pumps available to which satisfy different operating requirements (e.g., pulsing behavior, flow rates, efficiency, pressure envelopes),
peristaltic pumps are frequently employed due to their ease of use and simplicity in exchanging the tubing components that are wetted.
Diaphragm pumps are another common choice, which may be preferred for certain applications because of the different mechanism of
operation (e.g., avoiding oscillations at low flow rates, reducing mechanical wear on tubing).
   Tubing should be chemically compatible with the electrolyte(s). For small electrolyte volumes (on the order of 10 mL and smaller),
long lengths should be avoided and, if possible, the diameter restricted (e.g., < 1/16″ ID) to minimize holdup. While it is possible to
employ a wide range of tubing for peristaltic pumps, those not designed for such purposes may disintegrate faster and lead to leaks.
Still, even well-designed tubing can leak. To facilitate easy replacement at the most-likely failure point (i.e., the section of tubing
compressed in the peristaltic pump), tubing is frequently divided into multiple sections, with one section dedicated for the peristaltic
pump head (e.g., norprene tubing), and the other sections of (often less-expensive) tubing selected for completing the fluidic circuit (e.
g., teflon or polypropylene tubing).
   Electrolyte reservoirs vary in size and function. Critical considerations might include volume, material(s) of construction (for
chemical compatibility, thermal tolerance), pressure rating, aspect ratio (as large diameter:height ratios may be challenging), and
options for ports (i.e., inlet/outlet, instrumentation connections). Often, we employ glass reservoirs with open lids for acidic or neutral
systems and polypropylene reservoirs for alkaline systems. Using hole punches, gaskets can be cut from materials compatible with
electrolyte (e.g., EPDM) to accommodate tubing for the inlet and outlet flow paths as well as for inert gases (vide infra); it is often best to
place the inlets on the opposite side of the reservoir from the outlets to avoid bypassing the bulk volume (e.g., inlet at bottom, outlet at
top). Additionally, stir bars can be implemented to ensure homogeneous concentrations within the reservoir. Improved sealing ap­
paratuses are sometimes needed for chemistries employing solvents that readily evaporate. For non-aqueous systems that require
sealing, we often employ 10 mL volume molded perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) jars (Savillex, 102–0010-01). More specialized reservoirs can
be used to address advanced challenges with flow cell use (e.g., removing headspace for gas to prevent volume imbalance).
    Finally, equipment to control the current or voltage supplied to the cell is required. Our device of choice is a potentiostat, which can
reliably perform many electrochemical methods useful in the analysis of cell performance. Increased precision, higher current
capability, access to a broader range of techniques, more mature software interfaces, and integration with dedicated instrument
ecosystems tend to correlate with higher costs. Alternatively, more affordable equipment, like a battery cycler or a power source, can
be used depending on the application of the flow cell.

2.7.  Alternative and additional ancillaries

   The preceding sections describe the basic needs  for operation. In certain  cases, additional equipment  is required  for
experiments—we briefly discuss some of these here to ensure adequate consideration of necessary componentry for a distribution of
experiments and to support more advanced campaigns. Gases are often supplied to the head space of the reservoirs or sparged into the
electrolyte. Humidifiers, vessels containing the same solvent to that of the electrolyte and a gas sparger, can be used to pre-saturate the
gas with solvent vapor to minimize evaporation from the electrolyte tank(s). Sensors installed in reservoirs or inline to tubing can offer
information about the electrolyte during operation [61]. Such measurements might include conductivity, spectroscopy, or mass-
transport limited concentration measurement (e.g., via ultramicroelectrode), amongst others. The specific need and applicability of
each of these techniques depends on the target research question, the chemistry, and sometimes the scale of the system (e.g., smaller-
volume systems can be more difficult to instrument). Exchange of certain components and/or modifications to materials or func­
tionality can also expand the type of and/or elevate the quality of data obtained from the cell. For instance, variants of the diffuser
design have been developed to implement reference electrodes and to facilitate elevated temperature operation by using a combination
of thermocouples, heating elements such as patch or cartridge heaters, and a feedback temperature controller [20,62]. Further, the
inlet and outlet ports might be replaced with alternative fittings to ensure gas-tight seals and facilitate elevated-pressure operation
[63]. The flow cell might be placed in dedicated enclosures to keep it in an inert environment (e.g., glovebox). Filters can be used to
prevent accumulation of solids in the system, which might damage the flow cell, pumps, and/or impede flow. Other choices are

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Part category | Decision | Recommended route | ROM cost comparison, qty. 1–3 | Key controls and rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6061-T651 through-frame chamber, 312 × 222 × 140 mm | **HYBRID: BUY roughing; MAKE finish** | Buy 5.5-in plate with the core waterjet-cut or bandsawn, leaving 3–6 mm machining allowance; stress-relieve/rest; finish-machine datum faces, bore, ports, and interfaces on the VF-4 using multiple qualified setups. Quote a local large-part shop as a schedule fallback. | **Hybrid:** roughly **$1,500–$3,500** including plate and rough cutting, plus about **25–50 internal hours**. **Turnkey online/job shop:** roughly **$4,000–$10,000+**, driven by material removal, several setups, inspection, and shipping. These are planning ranges, not live quotations. | The 312 mm length fits the VF-4 travel, but the 140 mm depth and R10 internal corners require long-reach tooling and careful setup control. Rough cutting avoids converting most of an expensive plate into chips. Machine opposing sealing/datum faces from a common datum scheme and inspect after unclamping. LSU successfully CNC-machined a solid-aluminum LPBF powder chamber in its university shop, but alignment and assembly adjustment remained important (pqac-00000029). |
| 20 mm 6061 floor plate and lid with Parker face glands | **MAKE** | Buy blanks waterjet- or saw-cut; face both sides, drill/ream locating features, and machine each O-ring gland and its mating datum in one final setup on the VF-4. Outsource only blanchard/grind/lap correction if flatness is missed. | **In-house:** approximately **$300–$900 material/blank cutting + 12–25 hours** for the pair. **Outsource:** approximately **$1,500–$4,000** for the pair with drawing-based inspection; online prices rise sharply when flatness, Ra, and reports are added. | These parts establish the chamber seal and tolerance stack, so retaining control and enabling local rework outweighs nominal quote savings. Specify static sealing surfaces at **Ra ≤1.6 µm**, no radial scratches or spiral tool marks, and explicit flatness; published static O-ring guidance permits Ra 1.6 µm but rejects scratches, pits, and spiral scores (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). |
| Door | **MAKE**, unless it is a welded/windowed fabrication | Machine a waterjet-cut 6061 plate in-house; finish the hinge/latch datums and sealing face after all major material removal. If the door contains a welded viewport or complex sheet construction, buy the weldment and finish-machine the seal face in-house. | **In-house solid plate:** about **$250–$800 + 6–15 hours**. **Turnkey outsourced:** about **$700–$2,000**, excluding costly vacuum viewports. | Keep hinge, latch, and seal compression in one datum chain; use hard stops so the hinge does not define final O-ring squeeze. LSU adapted an existing chamber with O-ring-sealed doors and required careful bolting, evacuation, and backfilling during operation (pqac-00000030). |
| 316L build cylinders, 25.4/50.8/76.2 mm H7 bores, 3 mm walls, welded flanges | **BUY specialty finished cylinders** | Obtain 316L seamless tubing with extra wall or near-size precision tubing; have a hydraulic-cylinder/honing specialist weld or receive welded flange assemblies, then finish-bore/hone **after welding** to H7, roundness, straightness, and surface-finish requirements. Ask for a separate quote using stocked honed tube, but verify alloy, wall, and dimensional availability. | **Specialist finished pieces:** roughly **$600–$1,800 each** or **$2,000–$5,000 per three-size set**. Purchasing a suitable stocked honed tube can be cheaper, but short-length 316L exact-ID/H7 material may carry minimum-order and cut charges. Buying a honing machine is unjustified for three pieces; attempting H7 with boring alone creates high scrap/rework risk. | Do not accept ordinary DOM as automatically H7 or vacuum-clean 316L. Welding a 3 mm wall to a flange can distort the bore, so honing before welding is unsafe unless generous post-weld correction is planned. Require actual bore map, cylindricity/straightness, Ra, alloy heat certification, weld procedure, pickling/passivation, and final cleaning. |
| 6061 heater blocks and plates | **MAKE** | Saw or waterjet blanks; machine heater bores, thermocouple holes, pockets, and mounting datums on the VF-4. Use the HRT210 where radial holes reduce setups. | **In-house:** typically **$50–$250 material + 2–8 hours each**. **Online:** commonly **$250–$900 each** at qty. 1 because programming and setup dominate. A university comparison found an internally produced aluminum part at about **$108** versus approximately **$305–$624** from external platforms (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). | Excellent fit for available equipment, and dimensions may change during thermal testing. Ream only interfaces that need close fits; avoid imposing unnecessary tolerances on heater-cartridge holes. |
| Macor standoff rings | **BUY machined**, or buy stock and make only with proper ceramic controls | Send to a machinable-ceramic specialist or precision job shop experienced with Macor; alternatively, turn simple rings on the campus lathe using dedicated carbide tools, dust extraction, light cuts, and inspection. | **Outsource:** about **$100–$400 per ring**, with batch savings for identical rings. **In-house:** low raw-material cost but potentially expensive tool wear, breakage, contamination control, and student/shop time. | Macor is machinable but brittle and dust-generating; edge chipping and thin-ring fracture make ordinary online CNC fulfillment risky. Specify allowable chips, concentricity, flatness, cleaning, and packaging. Keep ceramic dust away from precision machine ways and metal-powder areas. |

{"answer": "# Make-Versus-Buy and Outsourcing Analysis for a Custom Lab-Built LPBF Machine

## 1. Instant-Quote Platform Pricing, Lead Times, and Pitfalls

### 1.1 Comparative Pricing (Quantity 1–3)

Documented comparative quotations from academic case studies provide concrete pricing benchmarks. For a medium-complexity 6061 aluminum FSAE suspension upright, Xometry quoted $305–$490 across four design iterations, Protolabs quoted $572–$624, and Fictiv quoted approximately $318–$326 (pqac-00000016). The same upright could be produced in the university's own machine shop for approximately $108 in materials (pqac-00000015). In a separate study comparing quotations for a cast-iron mounting bracket, Xometry quoted NZD 473, Protolabs NZD 605, and RapidDirect NZD 447; for a simpler pneumatic valve, Xometry quoted NZD 155, RapidDirect NZD 136, and Protolabs NZD 349, demonstrating that pricing differences between platforms are part-geometry-dependent and can vary by factors of 2–4× (pqac-00000001).

### 1.2 Lead Times

Reported standard shipping lead times were approximately 7 business days for Protolabs, 10 days for Fictiv, and 15 days for Xometry (pqac-00000015). Outsourced additive-manufacturing and CNC parts generally quote lead times of 2–10 days for production, depending on part size and quantity (pqac-00000018). Protolabs emphasizes automated quoting and manufacturing systems capable of delivering "within days" (pqac-00000017), while expedited delivery generally carries a premium (pqac-00000002).

### 1.3 Pitfalls for Vacuum-Sealing Parts

Online manufacturing platforms operate through two fundamentally different models: Protolabs manufactures in-house with its own equipment, while Xometry operates as a marketplace connecting customers with external suppliers, scoring them on quality, on-time delivery, and communication (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000017). Quotation differences between platforms stem primarily from differing assumptions about tolerances and finishing, as well as different pricing algorithms (pqac-00000001). Setup and programming costs dominate quantity-1 orders, and suppliers allocate these costs differently between setup charges and per-piece cycle rates (pqac-00000034).

For vacuum-sealing parts specifically, the following pitfalls should be anticipated:

- **O-ring gland surface finish**: Published O-ring guidance specifies that grooves, scratches, pit marks, concentric marks, and spiral machining scores are fundamentally unacceptable on sealing surfaces. For static sealing (face glands), the recommended limits are Ra ≤ 1.6 µm (Rt ≤ 10.0 µm, Rz ≤ 6.3 µm); for dynamic sealing (piston bores), Ra ≤ 0.4 µm (Rt ≤ 2.5 µm, Rz ≤ 1.6 µm), with spiral-free grinding specified for dynamic surfaces (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). The industry standard roughness average for O-ring gland surfaces has historically been 32 Ra (microinch, approximately Ra 0.8 µm), with relaxed specifications allowing 63 Ra (approximately Ra 1.6 µm) for static seals (pqac-00000012).
- **Automated DFM limitations**: Online platforms may reject or misquote deep blind pockets, inaccessible O-ring gland geometries, unusual thread specifications, and features requiring specialized fixturing.
- **Material certification and traceability**: Standard online quoting does not automatically include mill certificates, alloy verification, or lot traceability.
- **Passivation and cleanliness**: 316L parts require explicit passivation specification (ASTM A967 or AMS 2700) and vacuum-compatible cleaning; these are not default services.
- **Inspection documentation**: Dimensional inspection reports, flatness measurements, and surface-finish verification must be explicitly requested and specified on drawings.

The following table summarizes platform characteristics and pricing benchmarks:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 2. Make-Versus-Buy Recommendations by Part Category

The fundamental cost driver for the make-versus-buy decision at quantity 1–3 is that setup, programming, and platform margin dominate outsourced pricing. University in-house fabrication costs approximately 2–5× less than outsourcing for parts that match available equipment capability—a university comparison found in-house costs of approximately $108 (materials only) versus $305–$624 from external platforms for the same aluminum part (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Louisiana State University successfully CNC-machined its custom LPBF powder chamber from a solid aluminum block in the university machine shop, with plates, rail components, and related aluminum parts cut or machined on campus (pqac-00000029). Assembly challenges included alignment, felt sealing against powder contamination, and wiper-blade rail leveling (pqac-00000029).

The following table provides detailed make-versus-buy recommendations for each part family:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 Honed Build Cylinders: Buy Versus Hone

The 316L build cylinders with 25.4/50.8/76.2 mm H7 bores and 3 mm walls represent the strongest case for outsourcing. The lab lacks a honing machine, and achieving H7 tolerance (e.g., +0/+0.025 mm on a 25.4 mm bore) with boring alone creates high scrap risk. Hydraulic cylinder tubes are commercially honed to Ra 0.2–0.4 µm with H7–H8 bore tolerances as standard products. However, 316L stainless steel honed tubing is less widely stocked than carbon-steel or chrome-plated hydraulic tubing. For the specified small diameters, options include:

1. **Buy pre-honed 316L seamless tubing** from hydraulic-tube distributors and weld to custom-machined flanges. Verify that the specific alloy, wall thickness, ID tolerance, and length are available.
2. **Buy near-size 316L seamless tubing** and send to a honing specialist for finish-bore/hone after flange welding. Welding a 3 mm wall to a flange can distort the bore, so honing should follow welding unless generous post-weld boring stock is left.
3. **DOM (Drawn Over Mandrel) tubing** should not be assumed to meet H7 or vacuum-cleanliness standards without verification; DOM provides better dimensional consistency than standard seamless but is not automatically H7.

Estimated cost for the three-size cylinder set fabricated by a specialist is approximately $2,000–$5,000, versus the unquantifiable risk and time of attempting precision boring on the campus lathe without honing capability.

### 3. Standard Vacuum Chamber Vendors

Standard vacuum chamber vendors (Kurt J. Lesker, MDC, Nor-Cal, Ideal Vacuum, LewVac) predominantly offer cylindrical chamber bodies optimized for mechanical strength under vacuum loading. The 312 × 222 × 140 mm rectangular form factor of this LPBF chamber does not correspond to standard catalog offerings, which are typically round cross-sections in CF, KF, or ISO flanged configurations. Kurt J. Lesker components (flanges, viewports, valves, manipulators, feedthroughs) appear repeatedly in documented academic vacuum builds (pqac-00000028), and the company supplies individual components, sputter sources, and custom fabrication services.

Custom chamber fabrication from these vendors is possible but typically costs $5,000–$15,000+ for a bespoke rectangular box chamber of this size, as the work involves custom drawing review, welding, machining, leak testing, and certification. For comparison, the academic builds documented in literature took different approaches:
- Bidare et al. (2017) used a simple Perspex (acrylic) chamber of 350 × 230 × 220 mm, sealed to a baseplate with a silicon gasket in a machined groove, adequate for inert-gas purging to <0.5% O₂ but not for vacuum service (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024).
- Griggs et al. (2022) at MIT purchased a Parr Instrument Company cylindrical pressure vessel rated to 1,900 psig for their high-pressure LPBF testbed (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006).
- Wen (2021) at LSU used a donated 16 × 16 × 20-inch chamber from the Chemistry Department, sealed with ISO-KF clamp connections and rubber O-ring sealed doors, evacuated below 150 Pa before backfilling with protective gas (pqac-00000030).

For this application (inert-gas LPBF, not UHV), the custom-machined 6061 frame is likely the most practical approach, as it integrates the build-platform opening, gas-flow features, instrument ports, and door interface in a single monolithic body. Purchasing a standard catalog chamber would require extensive adaptation and would likely cost more than in-house machining of the designed frame.

### 4. Typical US Shop Rates (2024–2026)

Academic literature rarely reports explicit hourly shop rates, instead providing complete part quotations or using time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC) frameworks with capacity cost rates (pqac-00000038). The following table provides budgetary planning estimates synthesized from documented quotation comparisons and industry benchmarks:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

Key observations:
- Norwegian CNC machining quotations for a stainless-steel gripper ranged from 5,624 to 7,296 NOK per part (approximately $500–$680 USD), with the variation attributed primarily to lead time (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035).
- Online platforms generate quotations through automated analysis of uploaded CAD geometry, material, and manufacturing requirements, returning cost, lead time, and manufacturability feedback in real time (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).
- Actual shop-floor costs depend on batching compatible orders, reusing remnant material, and whether machines already have the necessary tooling installed (pqac-00000034).

### 5. Lessons from Labs That Built Custom LPBF and Inert-Gas Chambers

#### 5.1 Chamber Sealing and Gas Control

Multiple custom LPBF builds demonstrate that achieving and maintaining low oxygen levels is a primary design challenge. The Bidare et al. open-architecture system reduced O₂ below 0.5% using a detachable Perspex chamber sealed with a silicon gasket in a baseplate groove, with inlet and exhaust ports for filling and cross-flow (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024). The LSU system required evacuation below 150 Pa followed by backfilling with protective gas at slight positive pressure, using ISO-KF connections and rubber O-ring sealed doors (pqac-00000030). Commercial GE Additive machines achieve O₂ levels below 0.01% in sealed argon-purged chambers (pqac-00000011).

#### 5.2 Gas Flow Design

Gas-flow design was consistently identified as a major challenge. The Griggs et al. MIT testbed required COMSOL simulations evaluating baffles, guide vanes, funneling, outlet enlargement, and secondary nozzles, with the final nozzle 3D-printed on a Formlabs Form 2 and validated with anemometers confirming flow speeds above 1.4 m/s at 12–15 NLPM (pqac-00000005). Optimal flow velocity is approximately 0.5–4 m/s across the build plate: below 0.5 m/s, porosity increases; above 4 m/s, powder denudation occurs (pqac-00000022). Honeycomb flow conditioners with length-to-width ratios of 7–10 are recommended, with inlet geometry critical to preventing backward-facing step vortices (pqac-00000022). Plenum geometry and final assembly alignment directly affect part quality because nonuniform flow creates stagnant regions and process variability (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022).

#### 5.3 Powder Contamination and Optical Protection

The LSU system experienced a critical failure when fine metal powder accumulated on scan-head mirrors after several printing cycles, causing power loss, coating damage, and thermal lensing. The powder entered through a fine screw used to attach the F-theta lens. The solution was replacing the gate valve with a 2 mm thick glass viewing port, which simplified operation but reduced laser power by approximately 10% (pqac-00000031).

#### 5.4 Assembly, Alignment, and Rework

Practical challenges consistently reported across builds include:
- Dimensional adjustment and alignment during assembly rather than relying solely on machined tolerances (pqac-00000029).
- Felt or flexible seals between moving platforms and chamber walls to prevent powder contamination of sliding interfaces (pqac-00000029).
- Build-platform kinematic constraint systems with adjustable elements to align the powder bed with the laser focal plane and permit repeatable removal and replacement (pqac-00000005).
- The need for iterative design modification—the Griggs testbed used physical 3D-printed prototypes to validate gas-flow nozzle designs before final fabrication (pqac-00000005).

#### 5.5 Outsourcing Implications

The documented builds reveal a consistent pattern: labs fabricated most structural and precision-fit components in-house at their university machine shops (aluminum plates, powder chambers, adapter flanges, platform assemblies), while purchasing specialized commercial components (pressure vessels, optical windows, scan heads, lenses, gas sensors, motion stages) and standard vacuum hardware (KF/ISO flanges, viewports, valves) from established vendors such as Kurt J. Lesker (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000005). This hybrid approach preserves iterative design flexibility for the custom mechanical interfaces while leveraging vendor expertise for standardized precision components.

### 6. Summary Recommendations

For this 48-part LPBF machine build with an estimated 264 shop hours (of which 116 h is CAM programming and 99 h is setups), the following strategy is recommended:

1. **Make in-house** (~25–30 parts): The 6061 through-frame chamber (after waterjet core removal), floor plate, lid, door, heater blocks/plates, and most brackets and adapter rings. ### 1.1 Comparative Pricing (Quantity 1–3)

Documented comparative quotations from academic case studies provide concrete pricing benchmarks. For a medium-complexity 6061 aluminum FSAE suspension upright, Xometry quoted $305–$490 across four design iterations, Protolabs quoted $572–$624, and Fictiv quoted approximately $318–$326 (pqac-00000016). The same upright could be produced in the university's own machine shop for approximately $108 in materials (pqac-00000015). In a separate study comparing quotations for a cast-iron mounting bracket, Xometry quoted NZD 473, Protolabs NZD 605, and RapidDirect NZD 447; for a simpler pneumatic valve, Xometry quoted NZD 155, RapidDirect NZD 136, and Protolabs NZD 349, demonstrating that pricing differences between platforms are part-geometry-dependent and can vary by factors of 2–4× (pqac-00000001).

### 1.2 Lead Times

Reported standard shipping lead times were approximately 7 business days for Protolabs, 10 days for Fictiv, and 15 days for Xometry (pqac-00000015). Outsourced additive-manufacturing and CNC parts generally quote lead times of 2–10 days for production, depending on part size and quantity (pqac-00000018). Protolabs emphasizes automated quoting and manufacturing systems capable of delivering "within days" (pqac-00000017), while expedited delivery generally carries a premium (pqac-00000002).

### 1.3 Pitfalls for Vacuum-Sealing Parts

Online manufacturing platforms operate through two fundamentally different models: Protolabs manufactures in-house with its own equipment, while Xometry operates as a marketplace connecting customers with external suppliers, scoring them on quality, on-time delivery, and communication (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000017). Quotation differences between platforms stem primarily from differing assumptions about tolerances and finishing, as well as different pricing algorithms (pqac-00000001). Setup and programming costs dominate quantity-1 orders, and suppliers allocate these costs differently between setup charges and per-piece cycle rates (pqac-00000034).

For vacuum-sealing parts specifically, the following pitfalls should be anticipated:

- **O-ring gland surface finish**: Published O-ring guidance specifies that grooves, scratches, pit marks, concentric marks, and spiral machining scores are fundamentally unacceptable on sealing surfaces. For static sealing (face glands), the recommended limits are Ra ≤ 1.6 µm (Rt ≤ 10.0 µm, Rz ≤ 6.3 µm); for dynamic sealing (piston bores), Ra ≤ 0.4 µm (Rt ≤ 2.5 µm, Rz ≤ 1.6 µm), with spiral-free grinding specified for dynamic surfaces (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). The industry standard roughness average for O-ring gland surfaces has historically been 32 Ra (microinch, approximately Ra 0.8 µm), with relaxed specifications allowing 63 Ra (approximately Ra 1.6 µm) for static seals (pqac-00000012).
- **Automated DFM limitations**: Online platforms may reject or misquote deep blind pockets, inaccessible O-ring gland geometries, unusual thread specifications, and features requiring specialized fixturing.
- **Material certification and traceability**: Standard online quoting does not automatically include mill certificates, alloy verification, or lot traceability.
- **Passivation and cleanliness**: 316L parts require explicit passivation specification (ASTM A967 or AMS 2700) and vacuum-compatible cleaning; these are not default services.
- **Inspection documentation**: Dimensional inspection reports, flatness measurements, and surface-finish verification must be explicitly requested and specified on drawings.

The following table summarizes platform characteristics and pricing benchmarks:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 2. Make-Versus-Buy Recommendations by Part Category

The fundamental cost driver for the make-versus-buy decision at quantity 1–3 is that setup, programming, and platform margin dominate outsourced pricing. University in-house fabrication costs approximately 2–5× less than outsourcing for parts that match available equipment capability—a university comparison found in-house costs of approximately $108 (materials only) versus $305–$624 from external platforms for the same aluminum part (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Louisiana State University successfully CNC-machined its custom LPBF powder chamber from a solid aluminum block in the university machine shop, with plates, rail components, and related aluminum parts cut or machined on campus (pqac-00000029). Assembly challenges included alignment, felt sealing against powder contamination, and wiper-blade rail leveling (pqac-00000029).

The following table provides detailed make-versus-buy recommendations for each part family:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 Honed Build Cylinders: Buy Versus Hone

The 316L build cylinders with 25.4/50.8/76.2 mm H7 bores and 3 mm walls represent the strongest case for outsourcing. The lab lacks a honing machine, and achieving H7 tolerance (e.g., +0/+0.025 mm on a 25.4 mm bore) with boring alone creates high scrap risk. Hydraulic cylinder tubes are commercially honed to Ra 0.2–0.4 µm with H7–H8 bore tolerances as standard products. However, 316L stainless steel honed tubing is less widely stocked than carbon-steel or chrome-plated hydraulic tubing. For the specified small diameters, options include:

1. **Buy pre-honed 316L seamless tubing** from hydraulic-tube distributors and weld to custom-machined flanges. Verify that the specific alloy, wall thickness, ID tolerance, and length are available.
2. **Buy near-size 316L seamless tubing** and send to a honing specialist for finish-bore/hone after flange welding. Welding a 3 mm wall to a flange can distort the bore, so honing should follow welding unless generous post-weld boring stock is left.
3. **DOM (Drawn Over Mandrel) tubing** should not be assumed to meet H7 or vacuum-cleanliness standards without verification; DOM provides better dimensional consistency than standard seamless but is not automatically H7.

Estimated cost for the three-size cylinder set fabricated by a specialist is approximately $2,000–$5,000, versus the unquantifiable risk and time of attempting precision boring on the campus lathe without honing capability.

### 3. Standard Vacuum Chamber Vendors

Standard vacuum chamber vendors (Kurt J. Lesker, MDC, Nor-Cal, Ideal Vacuum, LewVac) predominantly offer cylindrical chamber bodies optimized for mechanical strength under vacuum loading. The 312 × 222 × 140 mm rectangular form factor of this LPBF chamber does not correspond to standard catalog offerings, which are typically round cross-sections in CF, KF, or ISO flanged configurations. Kurt J. Lesker components (flanges, viewports, valves, manipulators, feedthroughs) appear repeatedly in documented academic vacuum builds (pqac-00000028), and the company supplies individual components, sputter sources, and custom fabrication services.

Custom chamber fabrication from these vendors is possible but typically costs $5,000–$15,000+ for a bespoke rectangular box chamber of this size, as the work involves custom drawing review, welding, machining, leak testing, and certification. For comparison, the academic builds documented in literature took different approaches:
- Bidare et al. (2017) used a simple Perspex (acrylic) chamber of 350 × 230 × 220 mm, sealed to a baseplate with a silicon gasket in a machined groove, adequate for inert-gas purging to <0.5% O₂ but not for vacuum service (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024).
- Griggs et al. (2022) at MIT purchased a Parr Instrument Company cylindrical pressure vessel rated to 1,900 psig for their high-pressure LPBF testbed (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006).
- Wen (2021) at LSU used a donated 16 × 16 × 20-inch chamber from the Chemistry Department, sealed with ISO-KF clamp connections and rubber O-ring sealed doors, evacuated below 150 Pa before backfilling with protective gas (pqac-00000030).

For this application (inert-gas LPBF, not UHV), the custom-machined 6061 frame is likely the most practical approach, as it integrates the build-platform opening, gas-flow features, instrument ports, and door interface in a single monolithic body. Purchasing a standard catalog chamber would require extensive adaptation and would likely cost more than in-house machining of the designed frame.

### 4. Typical US Shop Rates (2024–2026)

Academic literature rarely reports explicit hourly shop rates, instead providing complete part quotations or using time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC) frameworks with capacity cost rates (pqac-00000038). The following table provides budgetary planning estimates synthesized from documented quotation comparisons and industry benchmarks:

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

Key observations:
- Norwegian CNC machining quotations for a stainless-steel gripper ranged from 5,624 to 7,296 NOK per part (approximately $500–$680 USD), with the variation attributed primarily to lead time (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035).
- Online platforms generate quotations through automated analysis of uploaded CAD geometry, material, and manufacturing requirements, returning cost, lead time, and manufacturability feedback in real time (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002).
- Actual shop-floor costs depend on batching compatible orders, reusing remnant material, and whether machines already have the necessary tooling installed (pqac-00000034).

### 5. Lessons from Labs That Built Custom LPBF and Inert-Gas Chambers

#### 5.1 Chamber Sealing and Gas Control

Multiple custom LPBF builds demonstrate that achieving and maintaining low oxygen levels is a primary design challenge. The Bidare et al. open-architecture system reduced O₂ below 0.5% using a detachable Perspex chamber sealed with a silicon gasket in a baseplate groove, with inlet and exhaust ports for filling and cross-flow (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024). The LSU system required evacuation below 150 Pa followed by backfilling with protective gas at slight positive pressure, using ISO-KF connections and rubber O-ring sealed doors (pqac-00000030). Commercial GE Additive machines achieve O₂ levels below 0.01% in sealed argon-purged chambers (pqac-00000011).

#### 5.2 Gas Flow Design

Gas-flow design was consistently identified as a major challenge. The Griggs et al. MIT testbed required COMSOL simulations evaluating baffles, guide vanes, funneling, outlet enlargement, and secondary nozzles, with the final nozzle 3D-printed on a Formlabs Form 2 and validated with anemometers confirming flow speeds above 1.4 m/s at 12–15 NLPM (pqac-00000005). Optimal flow velocity is approximately 0.5–4 m/s across the build plate: below 0.5 m/s, porosity increases; above 4 m/s, powder denudation occurs (pqac-00000022). Honeycomb flow conditioners with length-to-width ratios of 7–10 are recommended, with inlet geometry critical to preventing backward-facing step vortices (pqac-00000022). Plenum geometry and final assembly alignment directly affect part quality because nonuniform flow creates stagnant regions and process variability (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000022).

#### 5.3 Powder Contamination and Optical Protection

The LSU system experienced a critical failure when fine metal powder accumulated on scan-head mirrors after several printing cycles, causing power loss, coating damage, and thermal lensing. The powder entered through a fine screw used to attach the F-theta lens. The solution was replacing the gate valve with a 2 mm thick glass viewing port, which simplified operation but reduced laser power by approximately 10% (pqac-00000031).

#### 5.4 Assembly, Alignment, and Rework

Practical challenges consistently reported across builds include:
- Dimensional adjustment and alignment during assembly rather than relying solely on machined tolerances (pqac-00000029).
- Felt or flexible seals between moving platforms and chamber walls to prevent powder contamination of sliding interfaces (pqac-00000029).
- Build-platform kinematic constraint systems with adjustable elements to align the powder bed with the laser focal plane and permit repeatable removal and replacement (pqac-00000005).
- The need for iterative design modification—the Griggs testbed used physical 3D-printed prototypes to validate gas-flow nozzle designs before final fabrication (pqac-00000005).

#### 5.5 Outsourcing Implications

The documented builds reveal a consistent pattern: labs fabricated most structural and precision-fit components in-house at their university machine shops (aluminum plates, powder chambers, adapter flanges, platform assemblies), while purchasing specialized commercial components (pressure vessels, optical windows, scan heads, lenses, gas sensors, motion stages) and standard vacuum hardware (KF/ISO flanges, viewports, valves) from established vendors such as Kurt J. Lesker (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000005). This hybrid approach preserves iterative design flexibility for the custom mechanical interfaces while leveraging vendor expertise for standardized precision components.

### 6. Summary Recommendations

For this 48-part LPBF machine build with an estimated 264 shop hours (of which 116 h is CAM programming and 99 h is setups), the following strategy is recommended:

1. **Make in-house** (~25–30 parts): The 6061 through-frame chamber (after waterjet core removal), floor plate, lid, door, heater blocks/plates, and most brackets and adapter rings. These parts exploit the Haas VF-4 with HRT210 and CNC lathe capabilities, allow iterative fitting, and avoid the 3–5× cost multiplier of outsourcing at quantity 1 (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000029).

2. **Buy outsourced** (~15–20 parts): Sheet-metal hoppers, laser guard, and plenum panels (via SendCutSend, OSH Cut, or a local sheet-metal shop); 316L build cylinders with honed H7 bores (via a hydraulic-cylinder/honing specialist); Macor standoff rings (via a ceramic machining specialist); and 316L plenum weldments (via a qualified stainless fabrication shop with TIG capability and passivation).

3. **CAM programming time (116 h) is a sunk cost either way**: Whether parts are made in-house or sent out, programming and drawing preparation are required. For outsourced parts, replace CAM time with drawing/specification preparation time, which is comparable but cannot be eliminated.

4. **Invest the saved outsourcing budget in leak testing and inspection**: Specify helium or pressure-decay leak testing for the assembled chamber, build cylinders, and plenums. The cost of one comprehensive leak test is far less than the cost of debugging a leaking system during commissioning."}

### 2.1 Honed Build Cylinders: Buy Versus Hone

The 316L build cylinders with 25.4/50.8/76.2 mm H7 bores and 3 mm walls represent the strongest case for outsourcing. The lab lacks a honing machine, and achieving H7 tolerance (e.g., +0/+0.025 mm on a 25.4 mm bore) with boring alone creates high scrap risk. Hydraulic cylinder tubes are commercially honed to Ra 0.2–0.4 µm with H7–H8 bore tolerances as standard products. However, 316L stainless steel honed tubing is less widely stocked than carbon-steel or chrome-plated hydraulic tubing. For the specified small diameters, options include:

1. **Buy pre-honed 316L seamless tubing** from hydraulic-tube distributors and weld to custom-machined flanges. Verify that the specific alloy, wall thickness, ID tolerance, and length are available.
2. **Buy near-size 316L seamless tubing** and send to a honing specialist for finish-bore/hone after flange welding. Welding a 3 mm wall to a flange can distort the bore, so honing should follow welding unless generous post-weld boring stock is left.
3. **DOM (Drawn Over Mandrel) tubing** should not be assumed to meet H7 or vacuum-cleanliness standards without verification; DOM provides better dimensional consistency than standard seamless but is not automatically H7.

Estimated cost for the three-size cylinder set fabricated by a specialist is approximately $2,000–$5,000, versus the unquantifiable risk and time of attempting precision boring on the campus lathe without honing capability.

### 3. Standard Vacuum Chamber Vendors

Standard vacuum chamber vendors (Kurt J. Lesker, MDC, Nor-Cal, Ideal Vacuum, LewVac) predominantly offer cylindrical chamber bodies optimized for mechanical strength under vacuum loading. The 312 × 222 × 140 mm rectangular form factor of this LPBF chamber does not correspond to standard catalog offerings, which are typically round cross-sections in CF, KF, or ISO flanged configurations. Kurt J. Lesker components (flanges, viewports, valves, manipulators, feedthroughs) appear repeatedly in documented academic vacuum builds (goodwin2026aflexiblesmallscale pages 6-7), and the company supplies individual components, sputter sources, and custom fabrication services.

Custom chamber fabrication from these vendors is possible but typically costs $5,000–$15,000+ for a bespoke rectangular box chamber of this size, as the work involves custom drawing review, welding, machining, leak testing, and certification. For comparison, the academic builds documented in literature took different approaches:
- Bidare et al. (2017) used a simple Perspex (acrylic) chamber of 350 × 230 × 220 mm, sealed to a baseplate with a silicon gasket in a machined groove, adequate for inert-gas purging to <0.5% O₂ but not for vacuum service (bidare2017anopenarchitecturemetal pages 2-3, bidare2017anopenarchitecturemetal pages 3-5).
- Griggs et al. (2022) at MIT purchased a Parr Instrument Company cylindrical pressure vessel rated to 1,900 psig for their high-pressure LPBF testbed (griggs2022atestbedfor pages 3-7, griggs2022atestbedfor pages 1-3).
- Wen (2021) at LSU used a donated 16 × 16 × 20-inch chamber from the Chemistry Department, sealed with ISO-KF clamp connections and rubber O-ring sealed doors, evacuated below 150 Pa before backfilling with protective gas (wen2021lasersurfacetreatment pages 22-27).

For this application (inert-gas LPBF, not UHV), the custom-machined 6061 frame is likely the most practical approach, as it integrates the build-platform opening, gas-flow features, instrument ports, and door interface in a single monolithic body. Purchasing a standard catalog chamber would require extensive adaptation and would likely cost more than in-house machining of the designed frame.
